Masad, who founded Replit, an AI app and website-building company, has championed the push to reinstate Huang. When a friend told him about a petition on Replit calling for the fallen CEOâs return, âI literally jumped in and did tech support for them,â Masad said.
Huang has been âa great voice on pushing back on the narrative that we need to lock down AI, that the only safe AI is a closed AI,â Masad said.
He added that not having Huang at Nvidia would be a âhuge lossâ and âpotentially bring about a world where thereâs only the frontier model labs that exist.â
Software engineering careers âan accident of historyâ
When asked about the future of tech jobs, Masad said on Monday, âThe modern career of software engineer is a bit of an accident of history.â Now, many of his customers have zero software engineers on staff. âI used to get attacked a lot for saying that, but now everyone agrees with me,â Masad said.
Ben Lamm, the CEO of the biotech and genetic engineering de-extinction company Colossal Biosciences, agreed, saying, âWeâre doing what we used to do with 80 engineers with, like, five.â
And Edwin Chen, the founder and CEO of AI-training platform Surge AI, said that his headcount will likely remain stable. âIf you look at the latest models, theyâre not just writing code anymore. Theyâre often coming with ideas on their own,â Chen said. âTheyâre helping our engineers understand certain kinds of security risks or architectural trade-offs.â All this, Chen said, means he doesnât see a need to hire product managers or expand headcount dramatically.
Masad said he still foresees hiring entry-level employees, in part because in the agentic era, peopleâs jobs are changing every three to six months. âYou need people who are willing to continue relearning their job,â he said. âAnd I think, you know, just because of brain plasticity, younger people are actually pretty good at that.â

- Published
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
A blow to Asia's AI boom
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.
One of those is Singaporean data centre firm Megaspeed, whose former director Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese spy. Calls for tighter export controls have grown after Nvidia's Jensen Huang admited to an affair with her and resigned as CEO.
Megaspeed, the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia, is accused of illegally smuggling chips to Chinese companies after purchasing them for use in data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
The company has denied these allegations, defended its business as "legitimate and lawful", and said it has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation". It also said Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director in late 2023 and left the firm last year.
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, however, has said Brazil and the four South East Asian nations "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion" of the chips that Washington wants to keep out of China's hands.
The new measures are aimed at ensuring sensitive US technology "cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centers in third countries," the bureau added. Licences will be issued on a "case-by-case basis", it said.
Countries like Malaysia and Thailand whose data centre roll out has been heavily driven by Chinese buyers could be hit hardest, says international trade expert Naoise McDonagh from Australia's Edith Cowan University.
But the new rules are unlikely to derail the data centre boom as a whole, says Reema Bhattacharya from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft, adding that investment backed by major tech firms and clearly identifiable customers should "remain relatively resilient".
Singapore was an early adopter of data centres but when it began limiting new construction, investment flowed to neighbours Malaysia and Thailand. Johor in Malaysia and Batam in Indonesia have also approved billions of dollars worth of data centres to catch the spillover demand.
These countries have been offering incentives such as cheaper land to attract foreign investment, including from Chinese tech giants Alibaba and Tencent.
But now, the region could find it harder to get hold of advanced chips.
The BBC has contacted Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand for comment.
Singapore said it is "engaging relevant US authorities" to understand the new rules better, and is "exploring how to facilitate trusted access" for local firms.
A spokesperson for Brazil's Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services said it is aware of the US announcement and it "is closely monitoring any potential developments regarding this measure".
Malaysia previously said it welcomes data centre investment but "will not allow itself to be used to get around export controls".
A headache for China
The new rules also come just ahead of Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week.
Beijing has made self-sufficiency in tech a national priority and needs the best chips to build powerful AI models.
Chinese firms DeepSeek and MoonShot have come close to US rivals like Anthropic and OpenAI. So much so that The Institute for Progress estimates top US AI models lead the best Chinese platforms by only about six and half months.
"This is despite US AI companies having significantly better compute access and financing," it said.
Still, China needs advanced US chips to ensure its best AI models are competitive, experts tell the BBC.
The new restrictions on South East Asia and Brazil have taken away "one of the more practical routes Chinese AI developers had to accessing frontier computing power," Bhattacharya said.
But tighter restrictions could also push Chinese firms towards domestic semiconductors and further drive advancement at home.
That has been a longstanding dilemma for Washington, McDonagh said: whether to keep selling chips to China to retain its reliance on the US, or restrict access and risk further spurring Chinese innovation.

The man behind a star-spangled bet on the soft power of the US dollar was born and raised in Berlin.
âItâs this incredible instrument of soft power, where we donât have to send the troops and the tanks [and] we can still influence whatâs going on,â said Ferdi Dabitz, the 25-year-old CEO of Augustus, a new Silicon Valley and America First-coded entrant to the humble world of correspondent banking.
Itâs hard to find a sleepier corner of global finance than the largely paper business of moving US dollars between bank accounts around the world. It also happens to be hugely lucrative â Citiâs Treasury unit, which rests on a network of licenses in nearly 150 countries, printed $7 billion in profits last year â which helps explain why Dabitz, a former Thiel Fellow, has bet that he can do it better than the big banks, with help from a bit of AI and a lot of dollar diplomacy.
âThere is a global competition for power and China is doing their own thing,â Dabitz told Semaforâs Compound Interest. âSo gameâs on â I do think Augustus can be the free-market, US alternative structure as a public-private partnership in the form of a national bank.â Strong international demand for, and easy access to, US dollars also helps keep a lid on inflation at home.
Dabitz bills Augustus, which raised $180 million in July at a valuation of $1 billion, as a challenger to Citi and HSBC without the clunk, a clearing bank set up for more nimble, fast-paced global technology businesses.
Dabitz, born and raised in Berlin, shares the US patriotism that has come to define many of Silicon Valleyâs founders, and its obsession with the Roman Empire. (Augustus is named for the former emperor credited, in popular culture if not in rigorous economic history, with inventing modern state-backed money.)
âA 19-year-old guy, he had no army, he had no money, and there were like five to 10 people in the Empire who objectively had a better shot of gaining power,â he said, channeling Silicon Valleyâs underdog ethos. âI think the joke with Augustus is like, âHey, is money broken again?ââ

A Palestinian woman in her 70s has been shot dead, and several other people wounded, in a village in the occupied West Bank where Israeli settlers recently moved in, the Palestinian health ministry says.
There are conflicting accounts of what happened. Local Palestinians said there was an attack by settlers in part of al-Duyuk al-Tahta, near Jericho, which is meant to be under the full control of the Palestinian Authority.
According to the Israeli army, there was a Palestinian car-ramming attack on an Israeli vehicle. It said rocks were then thrown at the Israelis, who opened fire in response. It did not mention the fatal shooting of a woman.
There have been high tensions in the area since a group of settlers recently set up a new outpost.
They moved into eight houses in the village on 4 November after buying them, they have said, in a secretive operation. The properties are in an area where Israel retains full security control.
All settlements are illegal under international law.
Palestinian reports said Fadwa al-Fahidat, who was 72, was shot outside her home on Monday evening and that, hearing the news, her son sped to the scene in his car.
He then collided with an empty Israeli vehicle parked outside his family home and settlers standing nearby were injured, they said. The settlers then began shooting, the reports said.
The statement from the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that "terrorists accelerated their vehicle toward an Israeli vehicle and rammed it", and then "exited their vehicle with weapons and attacked and harmed the occupants of the Israeli vehicle".
Afterwards, it said, "rocks were hurled at the Israelis, who responded by firing in order to remove the threat."
The IDF said that Israeli security forces were sent to the scene and were pursuing suspects.
Doctors at a hospital in Jericho said that al-Fahidat was shot in the head. Several other Palestinians and Israelis were injured, reports said.
The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem says there has been a prolonged campaign of settler attacks, intimidation and land seizures in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, with Israeli troops now stationed nearby to secure the new settlement.
Residents and activists say armed settlers walk and drive quad bikes around the neighbourhood as they threaten Palestinian residents.
In a separate incident on Monday evening, eight Palestinians were injured when they were hit by a vehicle driven by an Israeli settler on a main road in Tuqu, south of Bethlehem, according to Palestinian officials and the Palestinian Red Crescent.
The IDF said the incident was a traffic accident. But the Palestinian foreign ministry called it a "terrorist attack", saying the driver hit a group of Palestinians who had gathered near the scene of an earlier traffic accident.
Also on Monday, the Civil Administration - the body that implements Israeli government policy in the West Bank - announced the allocation of more than 28 sq km (6,945 acres) of land in the northern Jordan Valley to nine settlers for grazing, according to the Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.
It said handing over vast tracts of land to settlers for grazing outposts constituted "direct support for the systematic expulsion of Palestinians from their lands and the rampant criminal violence in the West Bank".
The UK government said on Tuesday that it was imposing sanctions on eight companies building Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
It is the first sanctions package since Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's pledge in September to respond to the accelerating rate of settlement expansion in the West Bank, which he said risked rendering a two-state solution unviable.

Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Moscow's war effort.
The Kremlin said it would rebuild the bridge "better than before" and that Russian President Vladimir Putin had been briefed on the overnight attack.
Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said the Pivnichnyi (Northern) and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges - key crossings over the Dnipro River - were closed after Russia hit Ukraine's capital overnight.
Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.
The damage after the overnight attack, involving missiles and drones, appeared to be far more severe than during previous strikes on the bridge, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.
Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.
Zelensky said the strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".
He said several types of Ukrainian drones as well as the country's Flamingo and Neptune cruise missiles were fired overnight during a "pivotal stage".
The Ukrainian president also said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.
Ukraine's state security service SBU said operations had "systematically suppressed enemy air defence systems" over a month, and said it showed "no Russian defence systems can guarantee the safety of illegal objects occupied by the invaders".
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said the roadway on the bridge is "out of action", with no vehicle able to cross it, and the railway section is still standing, but with a damaged arch.
The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and illegally annexed Ukraine's southern peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Putin in 2018.
While Kyiv has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.
The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to China.
Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".
For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.
Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water supplies.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground metro services were damaged in the overnight attacks, local officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the central Cherkasy region, according to local officials.
The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.
The collapse of the arched section has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia â at least until the crossing can be repaired.
However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of Ukraine's southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Kyiv has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.
This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.
There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea with the Sea of Azov. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.
Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.
In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge â particularly its enormous arch â may have blocked the shipping channel.
This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for the Russian-occupied ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

For the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a new set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.
Kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up new versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.
A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.
Now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.
How kratom works
Kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, says Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.
In the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi says. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.
The leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most important is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.
Mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.
“It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” says Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”
Mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, says Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.
Labels may lie
What nature made, chemists and users are happy to tweak.
As the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann says, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.
When people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.
While 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.
What is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving users in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.
It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman says.
Kratom’s risks and confusing regulation
Sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she says. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.
Now, it’s a different story, Sethi says.
Patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she says. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.
VenÃ¢ncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.
Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.
Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.
Mondlane arrived at the Supreme Court early on Tuesday with "great peace of mind", and was greeted by dozens of supporters.
"As you can see, I arrive calm, confident in the work of my legal team," he told journalists gathered outside court, amid a heavy police presence.
The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.
"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.
Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.
The demonstrations continued for months, with rights groups accusing security forces of using excessive force against protesters.
Amnesty International, citing local civil society organisations, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, which was one of the country's worst post-election crises since independence.
Mozambican police put the death toll at 96, including 17 police officers.
European Union election observers also reported irregularities in the October 2024 vote, raising questions about the credibility of the results.
Prosecutors accuse Mondlane of encouraging demonstrations that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security.
The charges include publicly glorifying criminal acts, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit crimes and offences linked to terrorism.
He could face up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge.
Mondlane has rejected the accusations, insisting that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency rather than encouraging violence.
His party, the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), has described the prosecution as politically motivated.
The Supreme Court has denied allegations of political interference in the proceedings.
A heavy deployment of police has been seen patrolling around the Supreme Court and major streets in Maputo ahead of the trial.
In a statement issued on Monday, Mozambique's police appealed to citizens to "preserve tolerance and peaceful coexistence," adding that the right to demonstrate must be exercised strictly within the limits of the law.
Police also pledged to protect people and property while acting preventively and proportionately in accordance with the rule of law.
The court has only granted access to selected media organisations, sparking criticism from journalists and press freedom campaigners.
Court officials say the restrictions are necessary because of limited seating capacity in the courtroom, but critics argue they undermine transparency in a case of significant public interest.
The proceedings are expected to be heard by five judges, with witnesses called by both the prosecution and defence.
Political observers warn that the trial could reignite tensions in a country still struggling to recover from the violence and deep political divisions that followed the 2024 elections.

8402278f32eb.text: Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios Nvidia's post-Jensen Huang era begins in earnest with the release of its third-quarter results after the close of trading Tuesday. Why it matters: Investors and analysts will be reading tea leaves and listening for hints about near-term changes the company is making (or expecting the government to make) as a result of Huang's resignation last week and the circumstances that led to it. The big picture: Besides selling the world's most sought-after AI processors, Nvidia is a giant source of financial backing to the AI ecosystem — buying equity, making co-investments and backstopping debt in companies ranging from neoclouds like CoreWeave to fiber-optic cable providers like Lumentum. Nvidia is also a major partner of the two AI labs at the heart of the boom, striking a deal to provide a backstop for an OpenAI data center in Ohio and planning to invest about $10 billion into Anthropic following its IPO later this week, according to its prospectus. Huang could make these unorthodox deals — some call them circular finance — because of his position as a co-founder and sole CEO of Nvidia. Now that he's gone, investors will be listening closely for any indication that Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress, plans to step back from Huang's strategy of using Nvidia's resources to bolster the AI sector. What they're saying: Analysts will also be tuning in to Nvidia's conference call for hints about how the circumstances of Huang's ejection from the corner office — after reports of multiple affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset — could shift global sales patterns over time. "Our biggest concern now is new scrutiny that may restrict some of its sales into certain geographies such as Singapore/Malaysia. In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue," wrote UBS analysts. "Greater scrutiny of NVDA Asia shipments that indirectly (via cloud) service China customers, or more conservative funding/product allocation to US emerging/neocloud customers could also impact market share," wrote analysts with BofA Securities. "While the findings of the independent probe by NVIDIA and Congressional scrutiny remain to be seen, one possible outcome could be enhanced export restrictions," wrote analysts at HSBC, in a note downgrading the stock to "hold" from "buy" last week, adding that "during the past six quarters, 11% of total revenue was from countries excluding the U.S. and Taiwan, which we believe could be the focus of restrictions." By the numbers: Few expect anything other than another giant jump in sales and profits in the report itself. (If there's a significant miss, the already wobbly AI trade would likely get another clubbing.) Zoom in: That said, we'll be watching data center sales, which are expected to nearly double to about $101.87 billion. Also, given the weakness in the market, Nvidia's guidance for overall revenue in the current quarter will be of interest. Wall Street analysts expect it to be $125.2 billion. The company offered full-year sales guidance for the first time ever last quarter, and any tweak to the approximately 70% Nvidia previously said it expected for fiscal year 2028 sales growth will be huge. The bottom line: This will be a very delicate earnings report for the interim CEO and the rest of Nvidia's team to handle.

People visiting a large illuminated sculpture of the Moon have said it is an "amazing" sight.
ArtHouse Jersey has brought Luke Jerram's artwork to the St Helier Methodist Centre until Sunday 29 November.
The 6m (20ft) wide display, which has been shown around the world, features detailed imagery of the lunar surface from photographs by Nasa.
Arthouse CEO Tom Dingle said: "Something that makes the most of a public space, that makes us think about the world around us, about ourselves, but also something that we can all share together all at once, is really exciting."
The Moon follows a similar public artwork display in Jersey in 2023, when more than 31,000 people visited the Floating Earth on Queen's Valley Reservoir.
The installation features light and sound displays, which ArtHouse said would allow people "to encounter our closest celestial neighbour in an entirely new way".
Nine-year-old Ava thought the moon was "cool" and "like a big spot in the middle of the sky".
Primrose Keenan also enjoyed the exhibit, saying it was "amazing".
"We saw the Earth on the lake as well a few couple of years ago and that was amazing too," she added.
Toby Balderson said: "It does make a difference being able to see everything in such detail.
"We always just see little snapshots of it."
Youngsters Aquila and Starla, who are sisters, said it looked "really good" and "very big".
Dingle added: "Sometimes to stop, to take a pause and to reflect on the wider things, to think about the world out there, is actually really healthy and therapeutic."
He said the exhibit also showed the importance of free public artwork: "It enlivens our public realm, it gives us something to do together.
"It actually can change the pace for a day. It can give somebody a moment to reflect and it can mean something different to everybody - and yet we have the same universal experience at the same time."

A Costa Rican journalist who denounced alleged links between politicians and drug traffickers in the Central American country has been shot dead.
Police said gunmen on a motorbike ambushed Camilo RodrÃguez, 50, as he was travelling in his car north of the capital, San JosÃ©, on Monday afternoon.
The independent reporter earlier said he had been receiving death threats from drug trafficking gangs.
Local media reported that it was the first murder of a journalist in more than two decades in Costa Rica. It comes at a time when transnational crime gangs are increasing their presence in the country, driving up its formerly low homicide rate.
The president of the Costa Rican Journalists' Association, Yanancy Noguera, said that "all evidence so far points to the silencing of a dissenting voice in Costa Rica - a person who published information about organised crime in the country".
RodrÃguez had been working as a journalist for several decades, both in radio and in print.
Most recently, he had been uploading videos to social media in which he named public figures such as judges, business people and politicians, which he alleged were corrupt or had ties to known drug traffickers.
In one of his videos, he alleged that the home of Costa Rica's President, Laura FernÃ¡ndez, had been constructed by a company that he said had links to a criminal gang.
FernÃ¡ndez, who categorically denied any wrongdoing, took the journalist to court, accusing him of defamation.
Reacting to his murder in a video message, the president strongly condemned the attack, calling it "a stain on freedom of expression".
She added that she had instructed police to do their utmost to "punish Camilo's murderers".
RodrÃguez had also tried to stand for political office, seeking to run as the presidential candidate for the Costa Rican Renovation Party in 2021.
However, his candidacy was rejected by the electoral authorities after the party failed to meet the necessary criteria required to file candidates.
Costa Rica's Attorney General, Carlo DÃaz, said that "silencing someone who reports on drug trafficking or corruption, in this case a communicator, is a signal we cannot tolerate in a democratic society".

Grand Theft Auto fans have waited 13 long years for the latest edition of the game to be released - and going to extreme lengths to be ready for its launch.
GTA 6 will be released at midnight on Thursday - and Victoria Evans, from West Sussex, is not leaving anything to chance.
She has her alarm set for 05:00 GMT, and has a day off booked. She says she put the game's release on her leave request form which was approved, she told BBC News, despite the fact her boss "doesn't know what GTA 6 is".
She's far from the only one. For the game's launch day, HR software company BrightHR, external looked at absence data from more than 1.2 million employees from 70,000 businesses across the UK.
It found GTA was mentioned in 4.6% of time-off requests by employees. Throughout November and December, it said an estimated 83,000 days had been booked off for the game.
And booking leave is only one of the ways fans are making sure for the big day. Others are buying a new console to play it on or even pretending they're halfway around the world to get early access.
Big demand
Market intelligence firm Sensor Tower estimates, external GTA 6 has already generated $1.18bn (Â£894m) from 12 million pre-orders - although Rockstar has not confirmed this.
Despite the option to preload the 212GB game, Jennifer Holmes, chief executive of the London Internet Exchange, said several UK internet providers including BT and Virgin Media had "increased capacity in anticipation of higher demand" ahead of launch.
Gamers have long been known to book time off work for major releases.
When Red Dead Redemption 2 launched in October 2018, social media users were sharing plans to take the day off, with one analytics firm reportedly finding, external more people talking about calling in sick for it than any other game that year.
Similar conversations took place ahead of Cyberpunk 2077's release in December 2020, with fans discussing, external taking several days off to play.
Some places have decided to lean into the trend for GTA 6 by offering incentives around the game - including the US Army's 3rd Infantry Division based at Fort Stewart, Georgia.
It gave some active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play the game when it is released in November, as long as they sign a reenlistment contract for a minimum of two years between 1 August and 12 November.
"The idea was to have a unique incentives programme that connects to what soldiers are interested in," public affairs officer for the division, Lieutenant Colonel Angel Tomko confirmed to the BBC in August.
"There are 130 soldiers eligible within the battalion, and 20 have selected this incentive as part of their reenlistment," she said at the time.

Moving to New Zealand
Aside from taking time off, some gamers have also been discussing a technical loophole which could give them valuable extra hours of play before it officially unlocks in their country.
Because GTA 6 will release at midnight local time in all regions, New Zealand will become one of the first places where it is available, due to it reaching midnight earliest because of its position near the international date line.
This has led to some investigating ways to "trick" their consoles into thinking they're based in the island country when they are in fact thousands of miles away.
According to Google Trends, searches for the "GTA 6 New Zealand trick" have surged by more than 5,000% in the UK over the past month.
Games journalist Vic Hood said many gamers would be looking to play earlier to "get in on the action as soon as possible", as well as to prevent spoilers.
"As New Zealand is 13 hours ahead of the UK, that's 13 hours of gameplay that has time to spread across the internet and potentially spoil some key story beats and in-game surprises," she said.
"Took an extra day of paid time off when I found this out," one fan posted on Reddit on the trick.
It also means gamers would be playing the game at the much nicer time of 11:00 GMT, rather than having to stay up all night.
But another Xbox user shared caution on Reddit, noting that while the loophole had been exploited for many years for other game releases, GTA 6 "might be the game where Microsoft finally does something about this 'exploit'" - which could include banning players.
GTA 6's developers Rockstar and publishers Take Two Interactive have not commented on the loophole, and neither have Sony nor Microsoft.
Louise Wooldridge from Ampere Analysis said both Microsoft and Sony had "rules governing regional accounts and purchases" for the Xbox and PlayStation, adding that Sony's were "slightly more restrictive".
Players who choose to use the workaround could therefore risk breaching those terms and conditions and potentially face restrictions on their accounts or lose access to their digital games.
Some gamers will have to wait even longer than their console-playing counterparts to get their hands on GTA 6, as the game will not be available on PC at launch, similar to previous GTA releases.
"Spare a thought for the PC users who will have to live vicariously through others' YouTube videos and Twitch streams," gamer Stephen Finn told the BBC.

To be a China âhawk,â Jensen Huang declared last year, is a âbadge of shame.â
The former Nvidia CEO was a proud dove, one who found a dovish partner in US President Donald Trump â quite literally, in a business sense. Together, they formed an enterprise that aimed to sell high-end Nvidia chips to China, with the US government taking a cut of the profits.
Their alliance represented the high-water mark of a Sino-US dÃ©tente â peak dovishness, where a prime consideration in the White House was expanding Nvidiaâs market share, not blocking Chinaâs AI ambitions. Asked on CNN if it mattered who won the AI superpower race, Huang replied âI donât think it does.â
That moment has come and gone. A trade that not only sent powerful chips into China via legal channels, but also billions of dollars of hardware illicitly through Chinese-funded companies in Southeast Asia â one of the most active, Megaspeed, set up by a suspected Chinese intelligence asset with whom Huang was having an affair â has run headlong into the hard realities of US-China strategic competition.
Their superpower rivalry is structural. Its main focus is technology and, whatever Huang says, AI has made the struggle existential.
At times, Trump has seemed confused about the geostrategic stakes. In arguing for a let-it-rip approach to frontier AI model development, he has several times invoked the China bogeyman by insisting that âWhoever wins AI, wins.â
Yet he pushed Huang and chip sales to China into the forefront of his diplomacy with Beijing.
In May, Trump scrambled Huang onto Air Force One at the last minute to join his business entourage in Beijing at a Sino-US summit, reportedly despite knowing that his intelligence services were aware of the Nvidia CEOâs potential links to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.
Then in September, Huang was at the head table with Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a state banquet in Washington.
Huang would likely be with Trump in Shenzhen this week at a meeting of Asia-Pacific leaders if he hadnât been forced to resign.
Instead, the prospect of the US Congress ratcheting up tech sanctions against China will hang over Trumpâs third meeting this year with Xi, and could endanger their fragile trade truce.
Beijing, at least, is clear-eyed about the nature of its competition with Washington. Although over the longer term Huangâs spectacular fall may hold back US innovation and economic dynamism â a plus for China â the short-term consequences of a tightening embargo on semiconductors and chipmaking equipment would be immensely damaging. For all its advances in critical industries, China remains heavily dependent on American IP.
In retrospect, as my colleague Reed Albergotti argued, Huangâs mistake was to get mixed up in politics in Washington, where he had a target on his back. His defenders see a conspiracy involving the US intelligence services to bring down Americaâs foremost business supporter of engagement with China. Elon Musk posted on X that he would sign a petition reinstating Huang. Epic Games founder Tim Sweeney said his exit showed an âApple firing Steve Jobs level of idiocy.â
The broader question is the appropriate role for US business leaders in forging a relationship between rival superpowers whose economies are nevertheless deeply entwined through innovation networks, finance channels, and human talent. US strategy, writes Julian Gewirtz, a scholar at Columbia Universityâs School of International and Public Affairs, âhas come to depend, to an extraordinary degree, on powerful private-sector actors whose incentives the government cannot simply assume will align with the national interest.â
In Trumpâs lame-duck presidency, that issue will be taken up by an incensed Congress pushing bipartisan bills aimed at China. The doves have had their time to shape the US-China agenda. Now, geopolitical gravity takes over.

- Published
The United States has confirmed it is investigating computing company Megaspeed, suspecting it of violating US export controls by helping to ship tech giant Nvidia's chips to China.
In a joint statement, the US Department of Justice and Department of Commerce said they had been investigating Singapore-based firm Megaspeed since 2024.
It comes after questions were raised about the possibility high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
Concerns emerged in recent weeks after Nvidia founder Jensen Huang revealed he had an extramarital affair, allegedly with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang. US authorities suspect her of spying for Beijing, which China denies.
Jensen Huang resigned from his role as chief executive last week following revelations he had two affairs.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and is suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
The justice and commerce departments said on Monday that "it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information" regarding the investigation.
Laying out a timeline, it said it began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".
In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia "concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed". In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its 'no sell' list.
Agents from the Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, then conducted an on-site check at Megaspeed that month and interviewed Alice Huang, who was chief executive at the time.
Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.
The Nvidia scandal has created tensions between the US Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed.
On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of the chips.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Huang has agreed to testify in Congress, including before the House Select Committee on China to discuss whether US national security was compromised by his affair.
The White House said on Monday it would further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.
The reported affairs by Jensen Huang created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a major company in the AI industry and central to the US as it competes with China for dominance.
In the statement, the US government said it would "bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred".
They added: "Sensitive technologies like semiconductors are among the most valuable and strategic assets of the US economy, and the Department of Justice and the Department of Commerce will remain vigilant in pursuing justice for those who want to compromise America's technological edge."

b16d704e72ab.text: Data: National Center for Health Statistics via March of Dimes; Map: Carly Mallenbaum/Axios The U.S. earned a D+ for its preterm birth rate yet again , according to the latest March of Dimes report card . Why it matters: Babies born before 37 weeks of pregnancy face greater risks of serious health complications, hospitalization and death in their first year of life. By the numbers: The national preterm birth rate remained at 10.4% in 2025 for the fourth year in a row. It marked the fifth consecutive year at D+ (which March of Dimes considers 10.4% to 10.7%). Zoom in: Mississippi had the highest rate at 14.9%. Vermont had the lowest at 8%. Rates improved in 23 states and jurisdictions, including D.C. and Puerto Rico, per the report that relies on CDC data. But only Idaho, South Dakota and Puerto Rico recorded statistically significant declines. Between the lines: Rising rates of chronic health conditions before pregnancy are one reason the nation's preterm birth rate remains stubbornly high, Michael Warren, chief medical and health officer of March of Dimes, tells Axios. High blood pressure and diabetes became more common among women giving birth in 2025. Both conditions increase the risk of pregnancy complications and premature birth. What they're saying: "It's not just about improving care during labor and delivery," Warren says. "It's really about improving their health across the life course." That means addressing chronic conditions even before pregnancy. What we're watching: Whether strategies including expanding access to doula care and encouraging low-dose aspirin use among pregnant women at risk for preeclampsia can help bring down preterm birth rates.

93bdc8eb0df6.text: So many government problems, like last week's nationwide aviation meltdown , are foreseeable ... and foreseen. Why it matters: Again and again, we choose to do nothing until a crisis hits. A big reason: These are huge, tedious, complex, unsexy, antiquated systems that require persistence and competence to fix. A big new problem: These systems are deeply intertwined with our daily lives, and highly susceptible to malfunctions, mishaps and AI-enhanced cyberattacks. They're boring until they're vital. The big picture: We have federal agencies and congressional committees designed explicitly to monitor, protect and improve these complex systems. But they've atrophied as power has been centralized in the presidency and congressional leadership, where daily political warfare rarely includes sober discussion of competence and essential interconnected systems. Here are a few of the foreseeable (and foreseen) crises that have been staring at us, many for literally decades: The skies: We've known for years that the air-traffic system relies on copper wire and floppy disks . We've seen and known the vulnerabilities through Democratic and Republican administrations. We've known the fix is expensive: $31.5 billion, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told lawmakers last year. At Friday night's briefing at the White House, Duffy said: "I want $50 billion ." The grid: We've known for a long time that our electricity is delivered through an aging patchwork system vulnerable to accidents or attacks. The nonprofit power authority NERC (North American Electric Reliability Corp.) warned this spring that the system is so strained by rising energy needs from AI and humans that it could jam up or break. The water: Drinking and wastewater systems are old and in dangerous disrepair — a huge risk to hospitals, in particular. In July , cyberattacks hit over 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota, with Iran as a likely culprit . The government's computers: Washington spends over $100 billion a year on information technology. Roughly 80% goes to keeping old systems alive. Eight of the 11 systems most in need of replacement run on dying languages like COBOL . The people who can read, write and fix them are retiring. The debt: We paid $1.052 trillion in interest last fiscal year. That's more than we spent on defense. The Congressional Budget Office sees the interest doubling to $2.1 trillion in 2036 . Every dollar of interest is a dollar that can't fix another crisis on this list. The retirement cliff: Social Security's retirement fund runs dry in 2032. Current law then cuts benefits by 22%, automatically. Medicare's hospital fund follows in 2033 . We have known those dates for decades, and they've been creeping up. Now they're just a few years away. The shriveled arsenal: Rebuilding the advanced weapons we've burned through in the Iran war will take years . Back in May, a paper from the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that replacing some interceptors used heavily in the war, including Patriot and THAAD anti-missile systems, would take three years. The minerals: China controls 91% of the world's rare-earth refining capacity, giving the other superpower a chokehold on vital ingredients of AI. We're one trade war away from slowing AI and the entire economy. The bottom line: When choosing and rating leaders in harrowing times, put a premium on competence. We'll need it. Go deeper : The chain-reaction era.

6b256a6ce083.text: The push to reinstate Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable. Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power. Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore? Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing. "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergei Brin, told Bloomberg . "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable." Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy. President Trump said Monday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Elon Musk has also backed the effort. Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan , Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney , Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke. Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return. Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset. That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have called it into question. Yes, but: Others have pointed to the fact that Alice Huang worked on behalf of Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer that took steps to help Chinese AI companies access cutting-edge chips. The company has been linked to more than $4 billion in Nvidia chip purchases also arranged nearly $12 billion in orders of top-end Nvidia chips destined for Chinese companies, according to The Wall Street Journal. In addition to the relationships, Huang also faces questions about whether he misled Nvidia executives . Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating Huang, CNBC and Reuters reported Monday. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to look outside the company for new leadership, while tech analyst Dan Ives has dismissed the idea of a comeback as unrealistic. Zoom out: Musk has become perhaps the most prominent embodiment of the superstar CEO, repeatedly defying corporate conventions and weathering controversies that might have ended other executives' careers. In 2018, Musk settled SEC fraud charges over tweets about taking Tesla private, stepping down as chairman but remaining CEO. After a Delaware judge invalidated his enormous Tesla compensation package , shareholders voted to ratify it, and the state's Supreme Court eventually restored the award. Last year, Tesla shareholders approved another potentially massive compensation package, underscoring their willingness to grant extraordinary rewards to a leader they consider indispensable. The Trump factor: Trump's return to the White House added another layer to the power of tech executives, many of whom cultivated close ties to a president whose decisions can affect their businesses through government contracts, regulation and trade policy. But this month's midterm elections demonstrated limits to Trump's political power, raising questions about whether his backing will carry the same weight going forward. Huang's fate will offer an early test, though any decision to reinstate him might reflect investor pressure as much as political influence. The intrigue: The campaign to restore Huang has echoes of Sam Altman's dramatic 2023 ouster and reinstatement at OpenAI, when employees, investors and powerful tech figures rallied to force a reversal. OpenAI's board cited vague concerns about Altman's candor and its ability to trust him. A subsequent review found that his conduct did not mandate removal. Charles Elson, corporate governance expert and founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, said Altman's departure was fundamentally a dispute with his board, whereas Huang's case involves specific allegations of misconduct. "What if they were to do nothing? Then you have no code of conduct," Elson said. Altman himself acknowledged the parallels Monday, telling a Semafor conference he has "personal strong empathy to a situation like this," but declined to endorse Huang's return. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine; heroes have flaws," he said, per Bloomberg. The bottom line: Huang's fate could help establish whether the era of the seemingly untouchable CEO is continuing — or beginning to encounter meaningful limits.

e20dd7a20ce3.text: Democrats marching into a debate over expanding Medicare are about to confront difficult questions about how far to go — including for seniors who are already in the program. Why it matters: Holes in traditional Medicare leave seniors exposed to out-of-pocket costs and affordability struggles, but making the program's benefits more generous may be prohibitively expensive. The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress. Though the election results reinvigorated progressives' push for Medicare for All, there are also less sweeping options for what expanded coverage should look like. How far to go — and what to call the plan — will become critical heading into the 2028 presidential cycle and likely determine whether Democrats can attract any Republican support. Driving the news: Lowering the Medicare eligibility age is emerging as an early front-runner for what Democrats may try to pass and defy President Trump to veto. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) called on Democrats to lower the eligibility age to 55 soon after the election, framing it as an "immediate first step" toward his long-sought goal of Medicare for All. Sanders also wants to add vision, dental and hearing benefits and strengthen children's coverage. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York on Friday threw his support behind that kind of package, as well as strengthening children's coverage, Stat reported . And groups of Democrats in both chambers have recently introduced legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age to 50. What they're saying: " Medicare for All is unlikely to be enacted in the near future, but the political push for it could prompt a debate about the services Medicare itself does not cover and the high costs current Medicare beneficiaries can incur," KFF executive vice president Larry Levitt wrote last month in JAMA Forum . State of play: Some Democrats are looking at other changes beyond changing the eligibility age. More than a dozen Senate Democrats have introduced legislation capping Medicare out-of-pocket spending at $5,000 a year. House Democrats' health care working group called for both a $5,000 out-of-pocket cap and adding dental, vision and hearing benefits within the first 100 hours of taking the House majority. Between the lines: More sweeping proposals for a single-payer system would result in a Medicare program without premiums or patient cost-sharing. It would instead fund care with taxpayer dollars. Traditional Medicare now requires seniors to pay premiums, copays and other out-of-pocket costs. It doesn't include dental, vision or hearing coverage, and there are no caps on how much seniors pay out of pocket. This lack of an out-of-pocket limit leaves Medicare enrollees more exposed to high costs than they would be in an employer-sponsored plan, on an Affordable Care Act marketplace or in a Medicare Advantage plan. That's why nearly half of seniors in traditional Medicare — around 13 million — buy Medigap policies to fill the holes. What we're watching: Combining expanded Medicare access with more generous benefits only drives up the price tag, creating even more pressure to find ways to pay for it all. Democrats who ran campaigns promising to crack down on corporate bad behavior will undoubtedly look to the health care industry to ultimately pay for the changes. They'd still face GOP criticism for adding financial pressure to Medicare's trust funds and speeding up the date of the program's projected insolvency. Incoming Senate health committee Ranking Member Rand Paul (R-Ky.) "is likely to play spoiler" to Sanders' Medicare for All ambitions, Capital Alpha analyst Kim Monk said in a note on Monday.

8f9f0823954d.text: Look past the White House renovations , the proposed arch and the golf course : President Trump's border wall project is hundreds of miles behind pace. Why it matters: " Build that wall " helped build MAGA. But with two years to go, tough terrain and mounting political resistance threaten to leave Trump's signature promise unfinished. State of play: At the current pace, the main wall won't be finished until late 2029, while Trump will leave office in January 2029. There are about 619 miles of primary wall left to build, according to data from Customs and Border Protection as of November 10. The Trump administration has picked up the pace — from 2.6 miles a week earlier this year to 3.9 miles a week between mid-June and earlier this month — according to an Axios review of the agency data. But much of the remaining mileage is in Texas, where local landowners are fighting back and Trump's biggest allies were swept out of power in the midterms. Zoom in: The Big Bend sector — home to the state and national parks, multi-generational family ranches and numerous ecotourism businesses — has become a hot spot of resistance to construction, galvanizing political leaders across the spectrum to speak out against any physical intervention. "Just about every Democrat running statewide came to the Big Bend," said Susan Hays, who was just elected to be a Presidio County Commissioner. "all of them care about the border, the Big Bend, and they're going to fight for our public lands." Friction point: Texas Land Commissioner-elect Benjamin Flores, who opposes wall construction plans in West Texas and Big Bend, says his office could leverage state-owned land to advocate for surveillance technology to monitor for illegal crossings, which would be less invasive on the land, instead of a physical border wall there. The state owns 31 linear miles of land along the border. "The federal government is gonna need cooperation from us to get other areas that they may want done [and] that would make more sense to have the wall in," Flores said. The General Land Office already reprimanded CBP and one of the border wall contractors for unauthorized construction in a cease-and-desist letter this July. Between the lines: Trump faces two main fronts of legal fights. Injunctions: More than a half dozen lawsuits are challenging the border wall in West Texas alone, building on legal fights elsewhere on the border and in Washington. Eminent domain: If local private landowner resistance continues, the federal government will also have to file individual eminent domain cases for each plot of land across the border. It has already filed some of these cases, including one against a church in New Mexico. Zoom out: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said at a press conference this summer that he was planning for a physical wall from "the Pacific to the Gulf of America this time next year." CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott gave an extended deadline to the end of 2027. Based on data shared by CBP, there would need to be a rapid increase in construction tempo to make this possible. What they're saying: Flores plans to tell administration officials to ease their aggressive timeline. "Let's be a little bit more careful because you know this is gonna stand there for a long time. Let's understand those ramifications a little bit more. But that is not to say that I'm not willing to explore all legal options at my disposal to make sure I am defending the best interests of Texas," he said. The other side: Art Del Cueto, a former Border Patrol agent and adviser at the immigration restriction group FAIR, argues that the border wall needs to stick to the original plan. "Now you've heard other individuals saying, 'Well, maybe we don't need it where you have natural barriers,' and that's understandable. But when you don't build in those areas, what it's going to do is it's going to create a funnel," Del Cueto said.

The Iran war will loom over President Donald Trumpâs sitdown with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week.
A senior US official said that the president plans to discuss the ongoing conflict in the trilateral meeting, which comes as Trump has signaled dwindling interest in a peace deal with Tehran.
Last week, Trump directed Vice President JD Vance to turn away from negotiations with Iran. Earlier reports that Vance was considering face-to-face talks with an Iranian security official were incorrect, a source familiar with the situation told Semafor. Trumpâs post aimed to make clear that the administration doesnât need a meeting or a deal, the source said.
Still, the war continues to weigh on the administration and multiple sources say the US president would not be opposed to an agreement, if he views it as positive for the US; the source familiar with the situation argued that so far, Iran has not negotiated in good faith.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries starts his path to the speakership this week on smooth footing.
Heâs not expected to face any serious opposition within the Democratic Caucus â and while progressive activists have protested him, progressive lawmakers are heartened by his recent pledges to expand Medicare and take steps towards universal healthcare (just donât call it Medicare for All).

84ce1146103b.text: Some Democrats see Angie Nixon's Senate loss in Florida as a warning about running too far left. But her results with Hispanic voters challenge that idea, an Axios analysis found. Hispanic-majority precincts that some feared would reject her politics swung more than 21 points toward Democrats from 2024 and gave her a slight edge over moderate gubernatorial candidate David Jolly. Why it matters: Democrats gained more ground in Florida than in most states this year despite falling short in the two biggest races. Whether they can finish climbing out of their hole will shape the party's 2028 chances in a state seen as a Republican stronghold. " There definitely was a broad blue shift, it just wasn't deep enough," Daniel Smith, a University of Florida political science professor, tells Axios. "But you don't get to these close numbers without non-party affiliates and Republicans voting Democrat." The big picture: Florida swung further toward Democrats than Georgia's gubernatorial race or Ohio's Senate race, yet Florida Democrats had a bigger hole to climb out of. Governor: Democratic nominee David Jolly improved on the 2022 margin by more than 18 points, nearly 6 points above the median gain across 36 states, and 2 points more than neighboring Georgia, where Democrats took the office for the first time in decades. Senate: Nixon improved on the 2022 margin by nearly 14 points, more than a point above the national median, and 2.5 points above Ohio's Democratic gains. State of play: Florida's five statewide Democratic nominees finished within 1.6 points of one another in two-party margin, the least ticket splitting out of the 23 states with both a governor's race and a U.S. Senate race. Nixon's margin improved in Hispanic-majority precincts by 22 points over Val Demings in 2022 and 21 points better than Kamala Harris in 2024. The shift showed up regardless of where Hispanic voters came from, in mostly Cuban precincts (R+34 to R+14), mostly Puerto Rican ones (D+16 to D+35) and Mexican and Central American ones (D+3 to D+44). The intrigue: Outside of Tampa, democratic socialist Ashley Herrmann flipped state House District 69. Zoom in: The swing was particularly noticeable in the Cuban American core of Miami-Dade. In precincts where 75% or more of the voter base is Cuban, voters favored Nixon slightly more than they did Jolly, data show. Nixon lost Hialeah by 31 points. Demings lost it by 59 in 2022, and Mucarsel-Powell by 53 in 2024. She lost Westchester by 34 points and Tamiami by 33, down from 55 and 54 in 2022. Between the lines: Jolly outperformed Nixon statewide, but only because he had stronger support among white voters and in the most Jewish precincts of Miami-Dade, Palm Beach and Broward counties. The left-wing Nixon held her own with Hispanic voters, though the party's Hispanic statewide nominees did better. In Hispanic-majority precincts, Nixon ran slightly ahead of moderate governor nominee Jolly (losing them by 2.8 points to his 3.2) but behind attorney general nominee José Javier Rodríguez, CFO nominee Annette Taddeo and agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins. By Axios' estimates, Nixon ran about 3 points ahead of Jolly among Black and Hispanic voters and about 4 points behind him among white voters. The results could mean the anti-communist and anti-socialist attacks against Nixon resonated less this year — the result of Trump's immigration efforts, Smith said. "The sentiments are still there, but it'll be interesting to see if [the results] were a wholesale move away from the Republican Party for those who turned out to vote or a backlash against the overzealous anti-immigration efforts by the Trump administration," he said. Yes, but: The results still don't have "the full picture" of who actually voted on Election Day, Democratic strategist Steve Schale told Axios Monday. They don't show if some Cubans found Nixon or Jolly's comments appealing versus other Cubans simply not showing up to vote, he said. An Axios analysis found ballots cast in Miami-Dade precincts where most voters were born in Cuba fell 3% from 2022, while they rose 7% countywide. The bottom line: For Schale, Democrats must focus on the "gap," or what it will take to lose a Hispanic precinct by 20 points instead of 30.

Will President Trump meet Kim Jong Un?
