d0d3c1b9bf0c.text: The White House is dropping Heidi Overton 's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration because of a lack of congressional support, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The decision means the Trump administration will have to find a new candidate to lead the FDA as HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. looks to advance his Make America Healthy Again agenda. "FDA nominee Heidi Overton lacks the support on the Hill to move forward with her confirmation," a senior administration official told Axios late Tuesday. Zoom in: Overton, a physician and deputy director of the White House Domestic Policy Council, was nominated by President Trump in August. She had drawn criticism from segments of the MAHA movement that saw her siding with health and agriculture interests and helping undermine Kennedy agenda. Antiabortion forces also questioned her commitment to tightening rules for prescribing the abortion pill mifepristone. The backstory: Her nomination faced opposition from Democrats and skepticism from some Republican senators, including Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the Senate's Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee. Cassidy said he had "strong concerns" about Overton's role in the administration's efforts to change childhood vaccine recommendations, which he called "almost disqualifying." What they're saying: "We need to go in a new direction at FDA, and everybody fully supports Secretary Kennedy's vision to Make America Healthy Again and get back to a more populist and common-sense approach to health in America," the senior administration official said. The White House had tried to shore up her nomination Monday, posting on social media an account from the former dean of the University of New Mexico School of Medicine supporting Overton's confirmation. What's next: The HELP committee had been scheduled to vote on Overton's nomination on Wednesday. The FDA has been led by acting Commissioner Kyle Diamantas since Marty Makary resigned in May.

7450cf1497b4.text: A string of major technology failures is raising new questions about the reliability and security of systems millions of Americans depend on every day. The incidents are said to be unrelated, but their timing has fueled concerns about whether something more is at work. Geoff Bennett discussed the wave of disruptions with Eric O'Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative. Amna Nawaz: A string of major technology failures is raising new questions about the reliability and security of systems that millions of Americans depend on every day. The latest incident involved the NSA, or National Security Agency, which said its own internal systems were affected by an outage today. The NSA said it happened as part of routine maintenance and did not affect security operations. But several news reports said the outage involved a classified internal network. Geoff Bennett: And this was the latest in a series of high-profile problems. In just the past week, a Microsoft outage last Thursday disrupted services around the world. On Friday, a nationwide ground stop by the FAA brought air travel to a halt. And, yesterday, United Airlines experienced a separate outage, while customers of several major banks, including Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo, reported problems accessing their accounts. The incidents are said to be unrelated, but their timing has fueled concerns about whether something more is at work. Homeland security Secretary Markwayne Mullin in an interview last night dismissed suggestions of a coordinated cyberattack, instead blamed artificial intelligence. Markwayne Mullin: So I started talking to the tech industry, and one guy that's very smart with tech -- he asked not to mention his name -- no, it's not, Elon, so let me just put that out. But I said, what could be causing all these separate allergies? And he says, I believe that it's the SI. He said, because these programs aren't designed to work as fast as SI is. And so when they contribute -- or when they put in a program that's able to write codes and it goes in itself fixes itself, that's a ripple effect. And it causes a systems to be overrun that weren't designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today. Geoff Bennett: But that is far from conclusive. For more on this wave of disruptions, we turn to Eric O'Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative, who's now a cybersecurity executive specializing in cyber threats and national security. Thank for being with us. Eric O'Neill: It's great to be here. Geoff Bennett: So we have seen a remarkable series of technology failures in just the past week. Understanding that, as we sit here and speak, there are more questions than answers still, what do we know about what's behind these disruptions? And is there any evidence that these are connected in any way? Eric O'Neill: Right. So, so far, no evidence that they are connected, other than there is a massive coincidence behind this, and I'll get into that as a second. And, unfortunately, we don't know a lot because each of the different organizations and the government agencies that have been brought down by this are being very not forthcoming. So we start with Microsoft, who called it a technical glitch. They did that under an abundance of caution. Then, the banks -- right after that, on the heels of that, banks start to fail and people can't log in. And then, of course, United comes back and says, we're having problems. I'm really glad I'm not flying this week. And then, finally, the NSA has a problem with one of their classified systems. You put that all together in this string of events -- and there are other companies that, by the way, in all of this have gone down -- and it's too much of a coincidence to say that there might not -- there might be some external factor causing all of these. That is what investigators are going to be looking at very diligently right now. Geoff Bennett: We heard the homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, say there's no indication these incidents were caused by a cyberattack. How confident can investigators be in ruling that out at this stage? How long might it take to determine whether there was a sophisticated intrusion? Eric O'Neill: They can't be confident at all. Right now, there are a number of different paths that investigators are going to look at,in fact, three things. They're going to be looking at whether this was just a coincidence of internal failures within companies that are using the cloud and are broadly used across the industry. They're part of critical infrastructure. Two, they're looking at whether there was an external attacker or force that came in and caused a flaw or a disruption based on some external threat. And, three -- and this might actually be the more likely one -- they will be looking at whether there is a common application, networking tool or technology that these companies in these similar industries use that broke down, went bad, or was attacked by an external threat actor. No matter how it happened, it still causes the same amount of chaos. So, investigators are going to be looking down all three of those paths to see which it was. And I would bet, within a week, by next week, by this time next week, we will know a lot more data about what they learned. Geoff Bennett: The secretary has also suggested that artificial intelligence is overwhelming older systems. Does that explanation hold up from a technical standpoint? Eric O'Neill: I think, yes, it does. But I would suggest that the artificial intelligence that is overwhelming these systems is not coming from within the companies themselves, but actually and, as we have se

On Wednesday, the president heads to China for meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. 01fef5d8b5b8.text: In our news wrap Tuesday, international health officials say the United States is no longer considered a measles-free nation, a Harvard study shows cellphone bans in some schools are leading to modest improvements in academic growth among students and maritime monitors say a gas tanker went up in flames in the Strait of Hormuz after it was hit by multiple projectiles. Amna Nawaz: In the day's other headlines: International health officials say the United States is no longer considered a measles-free nation. In a virtual briefing today, the Pan American Health Organization said endemic measles outbreaks in the U.S., along with Mexico and Bolivia, signaled the reemergence of a disease that was once seen as controlled. Dr. Jarbas Barbosa (through interpreter): Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world. Measles' elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf. It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community. Amna Nawaz: The measles elimination status is largely symbolic. Still, the Pan American Health Organization said it expects the three nations to submit plans in the coming weeks on how they will try to stop transmission for at least a year. Measles have been spreading in the U.S. at the highest rate in more than 30 years, mostly among the unvaccinated. Today, CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz stressed the importance of vaccination. Cell phone bans in some U.S. schools are leading to -- quote -- "modest improvements" in academic growth among students. That's according to a new study led by Harvard University. The report says strict cell phone bans, like using lockable pouches, restore the equivalent of one to two weeks of learning each year. But that's only about half the annual decline in test scores we have seen over the past decade or so. The study is the first nationwide assessment of its kind, analyzing math and reading scores of more than three million students at some 4,600 schools. Turning now to the war in Iran, maritime monitors say a gas tanker went up in flames today in the Strait of Hormuz after it was hit by multiple projectiles. The crew had to abandon ship after it was engulfed by an inferno off the coast of Oman. Separately, Bahrain says it intercepted a flurry of Iranian drones that were headed toward a U.S. radar facility. U.S. Central Command reported no damage or injuries. In the meantime, a third carrier group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is now in the region, even as concerns linger over long deployments. Appearing in front of the Senate Armed Services Committee today, President Trump's pick to lead the Navy, current Acting Secretary Hung Cao, addressed a prior deployment, the USS Lincoln, which saw a number of suicide attempts during its record-setting time at sea. Hung Cao: I did answer those inquiries right away, especially with the mental health issues. You see it as eight suicide attempts. I see it as eight suicide mitigations because of the chaplains we have on board, the deployment resiliency counselors, as well as mental health specialists. Amna Nawaz: Cao also acknowledged the Iran war's strain on Navy resources, but insisted that joint operations with other U.S. military branches have sent a message to adversaries like China. In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says his country's drones and missiles hit a bridge linking Russia with the occupied Crimean Peninsula, calling the attack unprecedented. The 12-mile Kerch Bridge is a vital artery for moving Russian military supplies to the front line. Video released by Ukraine's security service shows drones hitting the bridge. Military officials say part of its road link was severed, though a railway line remains intact. A Kremlin spokesperson says the bridge will be restored. In the meantime, Russia fired missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two bridges there and killing at least two people. In corporate news, Nvidia beat expectations in its first earnings report since CEO Jensen Huang stepped down. The AI giant reported revenues of nearly $116 billion in the last quarter, more than double what it made a year earlier. And the company's expecting even higher revenues in the current quarter. Those results came after the closing bell on Wall Street. Before that, stocks struggled once again, with the Dow Jones industrial average dropping by nearly 850 points. The Nasdaq fell by almost three-quarters-of-a-percent. The S&P 500 posted its lowest close since July. And on Australia's Christmas Island, tens of millions of red crabs have begun their annual migration in one of nature's most unique and stunning sites. Dubbed the Ruby Red Rush Hour, the crabs make their way from the forest to the ocean to breed. Local authorities say the exact timing and speed of the migration is determined by the phases of the moon. Officials clear roads and even build bridges to help ensure a smooth journey. Naturalist David Attenborough has described it as a -- quote -- "great scarlet curtain, moving down the cliffs and rocks towards the sea." Couldn't have said it better of ourselves.

41201adbe721.text: The Trump administration is seeking $50 billion to modernize the nation's air traffic control system following last week's massive nationwide ground stop. But the proposal could face resistance in Congress, where lawmakers are raising questions about the cost and how the money would be spent. Congressional correspondent Lisa Desjardins breaks down the price tag and the political hurdles ahead. Geoff Bennett: The Trump administration is seeking $50 billion to modernize the nation's air traffic control system following last week's massive nationwide ground stop. But the proposal could face resistance in Congress, where lawmakers are raising questions about the cost and how that money would be spent. Our congressional correspondent, Lisa Desjardins, joins us now to break down the price tag and the political hurdles ahead. So, Lisa, how did Secretary Duffy, how is he explaining this $50 billion he's seeking and his decision-making over the weekend with this ground stop? Lisa Desjardins: He has been calling some congressional leaders and he had lunch today with Senate Republicans. He again reiterated that it is was a faulty router made by Juniper Networks that was to blame. However, he and the FAA administrator told the press today they're not sure exactly why that router misfired. They have taken this report, and they have gone forward and shut down all of the Juniper Network routers in the system so far. As to that ground stop, he defended that decision. He said it was critical for safety. Sean Duffy: I get like it was hard for people. But I would rather have that story than the other story that we didn't do our job, and we let risk into the system, but we kept flying, because then all of you would say, why didn't you shut it down? Why didn't you make that decision? Lisa Desjardins: Now he is trying to encourage Congress to make a different decision, which, as you say, is fund $50 billion. We were one of the first outlets to get a copy of that proposal for Congress. It's just two pages, look at that, but $50 billion. Here's what the secretary wants, $20 billion, first of all, for new terminals and upgrades at some airports around the country, $10 billion for air traffic control towers, and some computing needs. Some of that is needed for that fiber copper wire switch, $10 billion for five air route traffic centers. Those are the centers that handle flights as they are overhead at high altitudes. This is a large ask. This is $50 billion, and it is also a late ask, because this Congress is getting ready to close down for its session. Geoff Bennett: So what's been the response from lawmakers so far? Lisa Desjardins: Yes. Talking to Republicans coming out of that luncheon, they all said universally that they actually do trust Secretary Duffy. I didn't sense that he has a threat from them. He still has their trust. However, they all have a lot of skepticism about this request. One senator told me he thought airlines should be paying for all of this. Another, Senator Kennedy of Louisiana, said he thinks that airports should not be something that the federal government is paying to improve. Geoff Bennett: Meantime, this Congress is in its final weeks. It's a lame-duck session. What remains on their to-do list? Lisa Desjardins: Oh, boy, it's a pretty hefty lift. And as you and I speak, Congress is getting ready to leave this week and won't be back until December. Then they will just have a few weeks left. Let's look at what's on that list, some big-time stuff, including, oh, keeping government funded. The deadline for that is December 10. And I have to tell you, Geoff, there are some real red flags going up that we could be in a situation for a potential shutdown. So we will be watching this very carefully. In addition to that, Congress needs to pass the next defense authorization bill. That usually is done each year, usually bipartisan. We will see. Then, after that, Republicans have a big wish list, another reconciliation bill, where they will hopefully get some agenda items in before they're out of power. But I have to tell you, I just don't see the serious discussions happening yet for them to get all that done, especially that reconciliation bill, in time. Geoff Bennett: And, Lisa, while we have you, what is the latest with the midterms? Lisa Desjardins: Right. Geoff Bennett: What races remain to be called at this hour? Lisa Desjardins: Such a fascinating election. Let's start with the House of Representatives. There was even a new race called today. And where Democrats stand right now, you can see 257 seats. They have picked up a seat in North Carolina today. You see those seven yellow dots? Those are the races that remain to be called. Of those, three of them right now are looking like they will be Democratic flips. So we're talking 260 or above for Democrats. Let's go look at the Senate. And you have just one yellow dot there at the bottom. That, of course, is the state of Alaska, where our friends at Alaska Public Media have had one of the longest election seasons in years. But, Geoff, that could end tomorrow. Mary Peltola has been picking up votes, and she is poised to end this election tomorrow with 50 percent. Tomorrow is the day Alaska will decide whether it needs to go to ranked-choice voting or, if she has 50 percent, she will be the winner. Geoff Bennett: Lisa Desjardins, thanks, as always. Lisa Desjardins: You're welcome.

543f81bba06a.text: Almost two years after leaving office, former President Joe Biden has penned a memoir about his time in the White House. “Promise Me, America,” is out, but Biden isn’t out doing the typical run of media interviews. Amna Nawaz discussed more with his former counselor, Steve Ricchetti. Amna Nawaz: Almost two years after leaving office, President Joe Biden has penned a memoir about his time in the White House. It's called "Promise Me, America." And it's out today. But the former president isn't doing the typical run of media interviews. Earlier today, I spoke with his former counselor, Steve Ricchetti, and began by asking him why he was here on Biden's behalf. Steve Ricchetti: Well, he's had to limit what he's doing in terms of a book tour and things like that, because, I think as you know and has been widely reported, he has a stage 4 cancer diagnosis. He got that last May. And so he's working his way through the part of this where he still gets pretty heavy doses of medication to help manage the cancer. It's -- it moved into his bones, so there's some pain and discomfort with it, and frankly, even affects his energy level. So he's not going out in the way that I think he would really like to with a kind of traditional book tour, and so a number of us who worked closely with him are going to try to share some of the load and do it. Amna Nawaz: You have known him for so long. You know him so well. He writes in the book, too, about the span of his career. He says: "I was elected to the Senate as a 29-year-old kid. I left the presidency as an 82-year-old man. I have seen the long sweep of history." You say he wants the book to speak for itself. So what is it he hopes to accomplish by putting it out at this time? Steve Ricchetti: He wanted to do this close enough to his presidency, his time in office, that he could speak with -- and remember the events and talk through what he experienced because it was still fresh in his mind. He waited until after the midterms because I think he didn't want the book to be the subject of what the political dialogue was for the midterm elections. He wanted this to be and, as it was, a referendum in many ways on President Trump's first two years in office. So it was timed to follow the midterms, but to be close to his presidency enough that he could talk about it in the ways that he had, very completely and thoroughly. Amna Nawaz: I mean, it is very thorough. It's incredibly comprehensive. Reading through it, I was reminded of all these stories that we covered, the chaos he stepped into in the pandemic, after the January 6 insurrection, all the legislative efforts I know you were deeply involved in, from the American Rescue Plan to the Infrastructure Act, the CHIPS Act, rallying NATO after the Russian invasion of Ukraine. All of these are detailed in the book. And yet, as I'm sure you have seen, it is his decision to run again that's getting a lot of attention as people are making their way through the book. He writes about that in the book. He says: "I believe I was the best person to do it, the only person who'd ever beaten Donald Trump. I felt I was the best person to do it again." I'm sure you have seen, as folks read this, one journalist in particular called his reflection on this "pugnacious, unrepentant, and unreflective." What do you make of that? Steve Ricchetti: I just don't think that's a fair criticism of the book, for the reasons that you just said. I do think it is now hard to remember. Maybe there's even some kind of psychological effect from what we went through during COVID, but that we forget that he really inherited as severe a set of challenges as any president in our lifetime. There really were three crises in our country. There was an international pandemic. Hundreds of thousands of people had died of COVID on January -- by January 20 of 2021. We were in an -- the economy was flat on its back. We were in an economic crisis. And, again, what you just pointed out that people have forgotten, it was two weeks after the January 6 attack on the Capitol. And, really, the heart of our... (CROSSTALK) Amna Nawaz: ... he was sworn into office. Steve Ricchetti: Yes, and the heart of our democracy was on the line, the institution of the presidency, respect for other branches of government. There was so much at stake in that first year of his presidency just to restore a sense of confidence and respect for the presidency itself and to reaffirm our reputation and role in the world. Amna Nawaz: And yet, since then, as you know, the party is still sort of reckoning with that decision of how his candidacy for reelection ended, what happened in the wake of that... Steve Ricchetti: Yes. Amna Nawaz: ... President Trump's reelection. And I have to ask, because I didn't see it in the book, but, in hindsight, as you know him and you speak to him, has there been any reflection on maybe I should not have run again, maybe this should not have taken a disastrous debate or an intraparty feud? Has that ever been part of the conversation? Because it's not in the book. Steve Ricchetti: It's not because, in April of 2023, when he made the decision to run again, it was a pretty straightforward equation in his mind. We believed we were making progress in the country. There was no question that we had, the country had endured real difficulty, real challenge. His leadership through that period of time, in his mind and in my mind and in the mind of those around him, we just believed we were making progress. We knew there were still challenges ahead and work to be done, certainly more work to be done with respect to the economy and prices. And he believed he was healthy and more prepared than anyone to take the next step and to lead the country for four more years. Jewellery, glimmering silverware, sofas and an air-conditioning unit. Three months after his wedding, Faisal Shahzad's home in rural Punjab is bursting with gifts from his bride's family, as part of the dowry.
But the most prized possession is tucked under the bed: a 340W solar panel.
"In the summer we ran it from 08:00 in the morning until the evening," he says, adding they didn't need to use grid power at all during the day. "We ran our air cooler on it all day."
Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers' fields to industrial complexes.
From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.
People used to gift motorbikes or other household items at weddings, Shahzad says. "Now they give a solar panel and an air cooler. It has almost become a must."
Alongside the solar panel he still uses the national grid to meet his energy needs, particularly as he lives in a house with his family and brothers' families, who often use multiple appliances simultaneously. But in a country where the average wage is just under 40,000 Pakistani rupees (Â£110; $145) per month, bills are becoming unaffordable, rising to 15,000-18,000 rupees.
This year, COP31 is pushing the world to move away from fossil-powered vehicles, boilers and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. And while Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, the national grid system is experiencing knock-on eï¬ects.
The power grid death spiral
The big pivot to solar wasn't driven by government policy but by individual Pakistani households. Most people we spoke to said they installed panels to escape soaring electricity prices from an often unreliable national grid.
Electricity tariffs have more than doubled in a few years, says Muhammad Hassan Dajana, industry liaison at Renewables First, while the cost of Chinese solar panels has "decreased by 93%".
"People have just found another way to be able to survive," says Energy Minister Awais Ahmad Leghari. "It's a very healthy thing. We have adapted to the situation. The people have reacted and responded in a very economically viable and efficient manner."
While the solar boom brings clear benefits, particularly for a country that imports huge amounts of fuel, there are worries too.
Pakistan needs to avoid the so-called utility death spiral.
When people buy less energy from the national grid, fewer customers are left to cover the fixed costs of maintaining it. That can force prices up - which in turn encourages even more people to switch to solar.
Over time, this can lead to a two-tier system in which those who can't afford to buy panels face ever-rising bills, while the national grid becomes an increasing burden on the state.
"You'll have a white elephant in the form of a state-owned enterprise that requires a lot of public funding to just stay afloat," says Dajana.
Pakistan's government says the costs are already being felt.
"In just the past two years, the exodus from the grid has cost the rest of the consumers more than $500 million [Â£378m] a year," says Leghari. "That's a very big burden."
The government doesn't want to pull people away from solar, he explains, but wants the grid to be more competitive to be able to offer better energy prices.
Private power producers, which feed into the grid, have been heavily criticised inside Pakistan for locking the country into costly, inflexible contracts. Producers themselves point to broader structural problems like poor grid maintenance as contributing to higher bills. Leghari says the government has renegotiated most of the contracts and is now focused on making the grid more efficient with better storage, less waste and more innovation.
Leghari wants the country to run on "up to 90% clean power" by the end of 2036 - including renewables and nuclear - with dependence on imported energy reducing from 26% to 4%.
Solar-powered business
But as the government tries to improve the grid, solar is still expanding with widespread adoption in industry.
Kohinoor Textiles Mills in Islamabad, which is powered by a sea of huge blue solar panels, is one example. Utilities manager Sabawoon Khan describes them as his "baby", pointing at construction work levelling the ground for more panels.
When the sun shines, the mills' hundreds of machines are powered entirely by solar energy, Khan says. The heavy-furnace-oil engines they once relied on sit mothballed in a warehouse.
But there are limits. When it's too cloudy or polluted, and during the night, the company takes more energy from the national grid. In the coming weeks, like other firms, it will start using industrial batteries which can store excess solar energy.
"We needed to reduce our energy costs and this was one way to do it," says Taufique Sayeed Saigol, the mills' CEO, who adds the plan is not to disconnect from the grid altogether.
"The state unfortunately doesn't have the resources so we can't really say that we blame everything on the state. We do some of the things ourselves."
Critics accuse the government of moving the goalposts on solar power. Previously, households could feed excess electricity into the grid and earn credits, which were then used to offset the cost of grid power when the sun wasn't shining. That policy changed earlier this year.
"Initially their policy was very helpful," says Arif Ehsan Malik, president of Faisalabad's chamber of commerce. "But then the policy changed. Now they have started purchasing at a lower rate and selling back at a higher rate."
Malik says that makes a big difference for small and medium businesses. Leghari counters that the costs of the initial model didn't add up; the electricity the solar producers put into the system was much cheaper than the electricity they ended up taking out of it.

283fe6bc74ea.text: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions in one year than the entire nation of Denmark, according to a new report from Harvard University. From May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2% of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of CO2. Amna Nawaz spoke with the study's lead author, Gianluca Guidi. Amna Nawaz: The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions into the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark. That's according to a new report from Harvard University. The study found that, from May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2 percent of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of carbon dioxide, a level two or three times higher than an earlier estimate in 2018. I'm joined now by the lead author of that study, Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, welcome to the "News Hour." Thanks for joining us. Gianluca Guidi: Yes, thank you for having me. Hello, everyone. Amna Nawaz: So, what was most surprising to you from this report? What really stood out to you in the way of the findings? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. So think about it, right? So Denmark is an entire country, and with millions of people, homes, hospitals, and industries. And we're talking about, like, comparable annual carbon emissions from just 403 data centers. So those are just like 400 buildings. And that's an extraordinary scale. And those facilities are just only a fraction of the industry and how the industry looks like right now. Amna Nawaz: You point out in the report too you weren't even able to capture all of the information from many data centers. So what do we not yet know about the impact that they could be having? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's a great question. The study dates back like -- it's almost a year-old by now. And since then, there's been, like, an incredible build-out. We have preliminary results of newer studies that tells us there are around 1,000 hyperscale data centers. So that's just more than the double of what we reported in our study. Amna Nawaz: So many more data centers, meaning the numbers in here, in actuality, now the scope of emissions could be much higher than your report suggests. Is that correct? Gianluca Guidi: That is correct. Yes, that is correct. And together with the emissions, you have the water consumption and potentially also public health consequences. So, in a way, we have that a technology that is actually moving faster than our ability to understand its consequences. Amna Nawaz: Tell us more about that, the intersection of the build-out of these data centers and the impact on public health. What are you finding there? Gianluca Guidi: Yes. In this specific study, we haven't addressed yet the public health, but what's happening basically is that, once you have a powered demand and a power that is produced at the power plant level, not only you're producing, we're producing carbon emissions, but we're also producing hazardous pollutants that travel and eventually somebody breathes them, and the effects for the health are pretty dangerous. And there's plenty and ton of scientific research about this. Amna Nawaz: The power pull as well when we talk about the power use in -- of these data centers, there are states you point out, like Virginia, Iowa, Oregon, and Ohio that account for half of the electricity use. Why is that and what kind of downstream impacts does that have for residents in the area? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, that's correct. So, basically, the states offer the infrastructure, the land and the electricity that large data centers need. But there's a catch. So the benefits of these expansion aren't necessarily felt by the same communities that bear its environmental costs. So, more electricity demands can mean more power plans and, therefore, as we're saying, more pollution and more pressure on local infrastructure. So those consequences don't stop at the data center's fence. Amna Nawaz: There are those who will argue, Gianluca, I'm sure you have heard, that we need to build out these AI data centers, that the country has to do it to remain competitive, that it's necessary for our economy, for national security, and that the impact of that on the environment or for residents in the area is a necessary evil, in other words. Would you agree with that? Is that -- can that argument be made? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, I see that, and there's a big backlash happening right now. I wouldn't call them like a necessary evil. I mean, I am an AI researcher myself, and I have to say I'm really excited about this technology and what it can do. but there are better ways to build it, so -- that might cost more, they might take longer. The question is whether we're willing to prioritize doing it right over doing it first. Amna Nawaz: The report, as you mentioned, is now several months old, almost a year-old. There are a lot of things you don't address in it. For the average citizen to understand how this might impact their lives, what are the questions you think need to be answered next? Gianluca Guidi: Yes, here's what concerns me the most. We're building this AI infrastructure faster than we can independently understand its consequences. So, our study, as you were saying, was just published, like -- but the data are already over a-year-old. So scientific evidence shouldn't arrive after the infrastructure, and neither should, I believe, the public participation. And the main concerns would be the water consumption, the electricity, so such that putting the power grid into like -- in strain and potentially therefore, as I was saying before, the public health consequences. Amna Nawaz: That is Gianluca Guidi of Harvard. He's a postdoctoral research fellow there focusing on AI and public health. Gianluca, thank you so much for your time. It's good

Senior arts correspondent Jeffrey Brown visited for our arts and culture series, Canvas. Jeffrey Brown: A late afternoon walk through farmland in rural North Dakota, for artist Christine Kirouac, a chance to get away from the distractions of everyday life and do her work. Christine Kirouac: It forces you to be alone, really alone, and alone with yourself and alone with your thoughts and alone with the corn and alone with the corn and alone with the soybeans. Jeffrey Brown: Alone with the corn. (LAUGHTER) Christine Kirouac: Alone with the corn. Jeffrey Brown: Because there's a lot of it. Christine Kirouac: There's a lot of corn. Jeffrey Brown: Indeed, there is a lot of corn on the endless prairie in this area. But less known, there's also art making in an old house in McCanna set amid a tree-lined oasis. Kirouac was here to work as part of an artists residency program. What are the particular struggles for you in this region? Christine Kirouac: I think visibility is definitely one of them, but the representation of Manitoba or prairie artists can be lacking in terms of exposure. Jeffrey Brown: The residency is run by the North Dakota Museum of Art, some 35 miles east in Grand Forks on the campus of the University of North Dakota. Museum director Matthew Wallace … Matthew Wallace: We're not MoMA. We're not LACMA. We're just a little museum in the eastern side of North Dakota, just doing what we can do. But also I think that gives us some freedom to do whatever we want to. We don't have someone looking down our shoulders, and we just kind of roll with what we want to do. The building was a women's gymnasium, and we moved in here. Jeffrey Brown: What Wallace and his colleagues want to do is have a museum with an international reach, but that also very intentionally serves its region, which it defines broadly, a vast, sparsely populated area of the Dakotas, parts of Minnesota, Montana, and Manitoba, Canada. For Wallace, this is personal. He was raised on a ranch in rural North Dakota, feeling far from any art center. Matthew Wallace: Growing up knowing that I didn't have access to these kinds of opportunities, that it was something that I really wanted to jump on board with and make available to communities that were interested in participating. Jeffrey Brown: He first came to work at the museum on one of its signature programs, creating small art exhibitions and bringing them into near and far rural parts of the state. Matthew Wallace: You know, the conditions are not museum conditions. Jeffrey Brown: Right. Matthew Wallace: So, we could be... Jeffrey Brown: Probably is put it mildly. Matthew Wallace: Yes, yes, I mean, we -- I have installed exhibitions in an empty tire store, a Masonic temple, a church, a community center. Once in a while, we will we would get an actual gallery. There are those communities that have really worked hard and done that. But we don't want to put those limitations on them. It's more about them being able to experience it than the conditions in which it's shown. Jeffrey Brown: But this is also a museum that very much operates in and highlights a global art world. Its recent exhibition Material Abstractions featured works by artists using a wide variety of materials from South Africa, Los Angeles, and points all over. Curator Anna Sigridur Arnar … Anna Sigridur Arnar: I kind of like, juxtaposing those different kind of -- think about geographic diversity. And I do that a lot, because, when I curate, I think about works, entering into conversations with one another. Jeffrey Brown: But here too, Arnar says, there is always an effort to highlight artists from the region, including those who've left to build careers in the larger art world, but still look back to their roots, in this show, a sculpture of deerskin and willow by Carol Hepper, a work by indigenous artist Terran Last Gun, and this by Susie J. Lee, who grew up in Grand Forks and now lives in Seattle. She returned to her home state in 2014 to document the impact of the fracking oil boom. Each column, says Arnar, is a kind of drill core, also with details representing an individual worker. Anna Sigridur Arnar: She was very conscious about making these approximately the height of a human and weight. My art installer can testify to that. These were really heavy. Jeffrey Brown: Earlier this year, Arnar curated a show celebrating the 10th anniversary of another of the museum's initiatives for Northern Plains artists, it's Art Makers Series, a program that offers a solo exhibition to artists who've received some attention, but have never had a major show of their own. Anna Sigridur Arnar: I think it can be a game changer. Having a solo exhibition in a museum is kind of the creme de la creme. And it will open doors, and I love being a part of that. Micah Bloom, Artist: For the past 15 or so years of being here in North Dakota... Jeffrey Brown: Micah Bloom, who teaches at Minot State University, was the first art maker to have an exhibition featuring work that captured losses in the 2011 catastrophic Minot flood, including books found in the most unlikely places. His 2015 show included large installations and other works that he says he would never otherwise have been able to make an exhibit. So, by getting that first opportunity t

Eduardo Castillo, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/china-and-canada-expand-tariff-relief-while-relations-with-the-u-s-are-strained Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter China and Canada expand tariff relief while relations with the U.S. are strained World Nov 17, 2026 6:20 PM EST SHENZHEN, China (AP) — The leaders of China and Canada agreed Tuesday on additional tariff cuts as they pledged for deeper ties and Ottawa navigates strained relations with the United States. READ MORE: U.S. and China release product lists for tariff cuts after Trump-Xi meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and both praised the strategic partnership they agreed to pursue this year and pointed to improving economic ties. Carney's office said in a statement that the new measures extend and expand an earlier agreement between the countries. Under the agreement, China will provide additional tariff relief on Canadian exports worth around 400 million Canadian dollars ($280 million), including frozen pork cuts, fish and seafood. In return, Canada will extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products by two years. The meeting between the leaders came a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to maintain an integrated North American auto industry. "Improving and developing China-Canada relations serves the interests of the people of both countries and is also conducive to safeguarding world peace, stability, development and prosperity," said Xi. "This is the right choice." Carney said that the exchanges between Canada and China have increased in the past months and praised that now there is "greater predictability and stability" in their relationship. "The stabilization of our bilateral trade arrangement is indicative of how we can work together more broadly, pragmatically, to solve problems," he said. Carney added that his country is ahead of schedule in its plan to increase exports to China by 50% by the end of the decade. Xi and Carney reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 6cf874e5b096.text: What secrets might a 194-year-old tortoise have for humans when it comes to living longer? William Brangham examines the remarkable life of Jonathan. Amna Nawaz: Finally tonight, what secrets might 194-year-old tortoise have for humans when it comes to living longer? Geoff Bennett: William Brangham examines the remarkable life of a much-loved tortoise. William Brangham: It's lunchtime for Jonathan. Man: And he gets the freshest produce. William Brangham: Jonathan is perhaps the most famous resident of the remote South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, where he's lived for most of his 194 years. Dr. Stephen Clark, Kallel Foundation: And he was born before the telegraph was invented. He was born before the lightbulb was invented. He was born before the telephone was invented. When Abraham Lincoln died, he was 33 years old. William Brangham: Remarkably, after nearly two centuries, Jonathan remains in relatively good health, says neurologist and longevity expert Dr. Stephen Clark. Clark recently led an examination of the earth's oldest living land animal. Dr. Stephen Clark: He is blind. He has cataracts in both eyes, but he's very mobile, and still has a very good appetite, and is very social still. So, we expect he could live quite some more time, for sure. William Brangham: How did you land on the idea of -- that Jonathan would be a useful subject to study? Dr. Stephen Clark: Well, first of all, Jonathan's kind of accessible. So a lot of the long-lived species, like the bowhead whale and the Greenland shark, are kind of difficult to get to. And so knowing Jonathan was on the island was critical, and we could get access to him. And then we wanted to get a blood draw, but the island is very protective of Jonathan because he's very famous on the island. And so they wouldn't allow us to do a blood draw, so we had to do a buckle scrape of his -- of the inside of his mouth. So that's how we got the samples initially is, we actually did a buckle scrape of his mouth. William Brangham: Giant tortoises can live 150 years or more on average, but few reliable historical or medical records about them exist, and many of them outlive the researcher studying them. And what is it, practically speaking, that you're hoping to glean from Jonathan that could be applicable to humans and longevity? Dr. Stephen Clark: Yes, so that what really Jonathan represented is the first time we were able to really look at a difference between two different individuals over 200 years. So we compared him to a 5-year-old tortoise. The secret we have sort of identified with him is, he seems to have somehow been able to keep his mitochondria very young. And the mitochondria are sort of like the powerhouses of the cell. They provide the energy for the cell. They also provide energy for all the repair that's done for the genome. And so by keeping his mitochondria young, we think it's allowed him to repair his genome over 190 years. And so that was really the kind of surprising finding that we found with Jonathan. William Brangham: Do you think that this research and all the other research that is ongoing in this field, do you think we are on the cusp of extending human life in a meaningful way? Dr. Stephen Clark: So there have been predictions about what the maximum lifespan is for humans, and those predictions have ranged from 115 years old to 122 years old. I'm a believer and the nonprofit that I work with is a believer that we can increase current health lifespan at least closer to that. Going beyond that, I think it's going to require a lot more knowledge about the biology of aging. But I think the increasing average health span and lifespan to around 100, I think, is very doable in the near future. William Brangham: In their study published in "Science" this fall, Clark and his colleagues wrote -- quote -- "These investigations have deepened our understanding of gene markers that potentially slow aging and inhibit cancer in these species." In the meantime, one easy lesson from Jonathan... Man: He does love his carrots. William Brangham: ... slow down and enjoy a good meal in the sun. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham. Geoff Bennett: The secret to a long life, taking it slow. Amna Nawaz: Ba-dum-bum.

cd81011a0f9c.text: Nvidia's interim CEO said Tuesday that the company will be "disciplined" as it decides how much to invest in neoclouds and other AI customers going forward. Why it matters: Nvidia isn't just the biggest chip partner for AI startups — it's a major source of capital . What they're saying: "Our momentum is real," interim CEO Colette Kress said on at the end of conference call with investors and analysts. "Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this." She said the company would continue to use its balance sheet and support startups and the broader AI ecosystem, but she made clear it won't be a blank check. "As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees," she added. In particular, Kress said the company would continue to be "disciplined and selective in our support" for so-called neoclouds . Those companies provide additional computing capacity to big AI players as well as smaller and regional operators. "Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world." CoreWeave and Nebius, two such neoclouds, each ose by more than 10% in after-hours trading. Zoom in: Kress didn't name-check any other specific customers but said the company would offer capital to suppliers to help them move quickly. Nvidia will provide financing assistance or guarantees to some "very strong customers," she said. The chip-maker will "look very deeply" into whether guarantees are needed and conduct "a lot of work to understand if those are the right types of investments we need to make." Catch-up quick: Huang resigned last week after revelations that he had a relationship with a woman who allegedly had ties to Chinese intelligence. She was also a major Nvidia customer and helped Chinese AI companies gain access to cutting-edge Nvidia technology while the U.S. had banned some chip sales to the country. On the call, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones through cold water on the notion of a quick return for Huang . "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," he said. The company said it wouldn't be taking questions on Huang's departure or its ongoing investigation into his actions.

Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.
Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".
"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.
The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".
Another 'spy balloon' incident?
For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.
The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.
It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.
Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.
Now that opening may be under threat.
History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.
Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.
But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.
The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.
"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.
"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.
The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.
"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.
Trump-Xi summit unlikely to collapse
Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.
China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.
Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.
The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.
He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.
Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.

e856d44f265b.text: By — Laura Ungar, Associated Press Laura Ungar, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/doctors-are-raising-concerns-about-u-s-babies-born-with-measles Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Doctors are raising concerns about U.S. babies born with measles Health Nov 17, 2026 5:52 PM EST For the first time in decades, U.S. doctors are sounding the alarm about babies coming into the world with measles. Congenital measles happens when a pregnant woman passes the virus to her fetus in the womb. It can lead to serious complications or even be deadly for newborns. READ MORE: Can the U.S. regain its measles elimination status? Here's what to know From the start of 2025 through the end of this September, 13 congenital measles cases were reported to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention during large measles outbreaks, according to preliminary figures published in a medical journal on Monday. "This is a brand new phenomenon," said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota's Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. The condition's emergence is driven by declining vaccination rates, which have fueled the virus's spread so much that the Pan American Health Organization is expected to officially announce Tuesday that the U.S. has lost the measles-free status it's had since 2000. In the past two years, according to the CDC, there have been more than 7,500 measles cases. "We're now seeing levels of measles that we haven't seen in 30 years," said Dr. Adam Ratner, a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' infectious diseases committee. "When you have measles under control," congenital measles doesn't happen. The preliminary case figures were released in a public health alert published by NEJM Evidence in partnership with the center Osterholm directs. The alert also said there were 112 cases of confirmed measles during pregnancy — almost all among women who didn't get vaccinated against measles beforehand or whose vaccination status was unknown. The alert said getting vaccinated before pregnancy and having high vaccination rates in the community "are important to prevent measles and related complications." CDC scientists authored the alert. Guidance on congenital measles from the pediatrics academy is already reaching doctors. And Pennsylvania's health department published an advisory last month for healthcare providers, schools, childcare centers and others in the state, which currently has the largest measles outbreak in the nation. A new reality allows congenital measles to emerge People gain immunity to measles by getting the disease or the vaccine. Before the shots existed, lots of people were infected by the extremely contagious virus in childhood. Later, high vaccination rates protected everyone. But a new and historic reality — shaped both by the success of the vaccine and recent skepticism about it — has triggered congenital measles. "What's happening is we have so many women of childbearing age who were not vaccinated in the last 25 years, nor have they ever had exposure to measles because for the last 25 years we have beaten it back," Osterholm said. "Now, this group is highly susceptible to measles." Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Doctors say the best way to prevent the disease is for women to get the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, before pregnancy. This protects the fetus too because antibodies pass from mother to baby through the placenta. Protection can last a few months after birth. MMR can't be given during pregnancy. Unvaccinated women who have never had measles and are exposed while pregnant can get a solution containing antibodies within six days to reduce the risk of infection and complications. Congenital measles can seriously harm babies If a woman gets measles toward the end of pregnancy, there's a good chance she will pass it along. An estimated 25% to 30% of babies born to someone who gets measles shortly before delivery may become infected, the pediatrics group says. READ MORE: U.S. and Mexico officially lose measles-elimination status Babies are considered to have congenital measles if they were exposed in the uterus and doctors find evidence of measles very soon after birth. Common symptoms include fever, jaundice and a measles rash. Severe complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and a rare condition known as SSPE, a brain disorder that generally develops many years after a measles infection and is almost always fatal. Ratner, who wrote a book about measles, said there are indications that kids with congenital measles are at higher risk for SSPE and may develop it sooner after having measles than other children. "That's something that sadly we're learning more about," he said. Doctors worry things may get worse if vaccination rates keep dropping. Outbreaks are considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate, but rates in many communities have dipped below that threshold. Nationally, the CDC said, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received required MMR shots. This puts many vulnerable people at risk, including infants too young to be vaccinated. The first MMR dose is routinely given at 12 to 15 months old, and the earliest babies can get the shots is 6 months in outbreak areas. "We need to get back to the point where everybody who can get vaccinated is getting vaccinated, and that's gonna take some doing," Ratner said. "It's going to be a lot of work on the part of pediatricians and public health institutions and lots of others. But it's an important thing for us to do." AP Medical Writer Mike Stobbe contributed from New York. The Associated Press' health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism

Police in the Philippines have asked prosecutors to charge Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC that police had filed documents requesting that Markle be charged on Monday.
Earlier this month, Markle, 82, was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material, from storage units Markle rented.
Markle, who is in custody in the US, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney for comment.
Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had asked prosecutors to charge Markle with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.
Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.
Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

c130833e0467.text: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's $50 billion request to overhaul the nation's air traffic control system is getting a chilly reception from Senate Republicans, who are balking at the hefty price tag. Why it matters: The pushback from within President Trump's own party casts doubt on the administration's ability to secure the full $50 billion, even after Friday's historic nationwide groundstop . Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters that Duffy "made a huge mistake" by originally requesting $30 billion for air traffic modernization, then later upping the ask to $50 billion following the groundstop. "Maybe he was taking orders, but he's smart enough to know better than to say, 'I need 30 billion. We have a catastrophe. I need 50 billion now.'" Kennedy said, adding, "We're not going to give them $50 billion." Both Duffy and Trump have urged Congress to move quickly on the funding, which the administration formally requested Tuesday. Driving the news: Duffy, along with FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford, pitched the funding — which include $10 billion specifically for air traffic equipment modernization — to Senate Republicans at their weekly lunch. "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related," Commerce Chairman Ted Cruz (R-Texas) told reporters. Cruz floated using the fast-track reconciliation process to secure additional funding for upgrading the air traffic control system, but said the administration needs to show it can effectively spend the $12.5 billion Congress already provided in the " Big, Beautiful Bill " last year. "Demonstrate that you can actually modernize, and come back to Congress when you need additional funds," Cruz said. Zoom in: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has also raised concerns about the unspent funds. "There's some explanations that have to be given as to why that number is where it is," Thune told reporters Monday. Thune poured cold water on using reconciliation to pass the additional funds, instead saying he would like to work with Democrats through the normal appropriations process. But Democrats are also expressing skeptcism about the funding request, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) saying Monday: "We want to give them all the money they need, but they've got to use it, and know how to implement it — and they don't." The intrigue : Some Republicans want the airline industry and other users of the system to pick up more of the tab. "I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We've given them unbelievable amounts of money," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told reporters. "One of the things that you could do is make the people who actually use it pay for it, just like they have user landing fees," Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) said. "I think in a nation with a $40 trillion national debt and $2 trillion annual deficits, that we're going to have to find ways to make the people who are using the services pay for the services," Husted added.

Rebecca Pinals hadn’t planned to study neuroscience. But as she watched her grandmother decline from dementia, the chemical engineer decided to apply her talents to the human brain.
At the time, “one of the big questions was, ‘how do we get access to it?’” says Pinals, of Stanford University. “I thought nanotechnology could be an interesting and useful toolkit to answer those types of questions.”
One key access point is the blood-brain barrier, a dynamic microenvironment of cells that helps keep pathogens and other contaminants out of the brain. It’s so good at its job that drugs for treating dementia have a hard time penetrating it. It’s important for researchers to understand this barrier, Pinals says, but it is so thin and fragile that they can’t observe it in real time without risking patient health.
Pinals and colleagues re-created the blood-brain barrier on a microchip. The team reprogrammed stem cells engineered from human skin, then coaxed the cells to form the barrier in a small 3-D chamber on the chip.
“As an engineer, this [system] is perfect,” Pinals says. “We love to take things apart and put them back together to learn how it’s made.”
Experts could use this scale model of the blood-brain barrier to figure out how to noninvasively access brains affected by neurodegenerative diseases. Pinals wants to use the device to investigate nanoparticles that could deliver drugs directly to patients’ brains.

3b512e5d8837.text:
Public health is invisible — until it’s not.
It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” says Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”
But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin says. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”
In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.
Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.
Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.
Domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.
Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.
“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” says Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.
The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.
Such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”
A preventable outbreak
On the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.
About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in New York and Wisconsin.
Measles’ improbable comeback
As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.
Measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.
The United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.
In the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy says. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.
Fading protection from measles, mumps and rubella
During the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.
