63e265b1d7a8.text: By — David Crary, Associated Press David Crary, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/muslims-are-projected-to-outnumber-christians-by-2035-as-the-worlds-largest-religion Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians by 2035 as the world's largest religion World Nov 18, 2026 3:25 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — Islam is expected to surpass Christianity as the world's largest religion by 2035, according to detailed projections released Wednesday by the Pew Research Center. Pew, which has been issuing authoritative reports on religious demography for 25 years, said both Islam and Christianity are growing, but Islam is growing much faster. A key reason, Pew said, is that Muslims tend to have more children than other major religious groups. "It's the babies," said Pew senior demographer Conrad Hackett, explaining that conversion and other ways of changing religious identity are much smaller factors than fertility rates. During 2020-2025, the fertility rate for Muslims was 3.1 children per woman, followed by the rate for Christians at 2.5, according to Pew. The average fertility rate for all other women was 1.6, below the level of 2.1 that's considered necessary for each generation to replace itself. WATCH: The potential impacts of the U.S. birth rate decline According to Pew's latest estimates, there were 2.27 billion Christians and 2.02 billion Muslims worldwide in 2020. Pew's new projections forecast that there will be 2.57 billion Muslims and 2.52 billion Christians by 2035. By 2070, if recent trends continue, there will be more than 3.6 billion Muslims and just under 3 billion Christians worldwide. The estimates are part of a broader Pew project examining how the size of major religious groups could change between 2020 and 2070. The projections take into account recent differences between religious groups' age profiles, fertility rates, and patterns of religious switching and migration. Among the many notable findings: Pew projects that the United States, within 40 years, will no longer have a Christian majority. Christians now account for 62% of U.S. adults, according to Pew, and will fall below 50% by 2065. WATCH: New PBS series explores the often-overlooked history of American Muslims In neighboring Canada, Christians are expected to drop below 50% by 2030, Pew said. In both countries, a significant reason for the drop is the concurrent increase in the number of people with no religious affiliation. By 2070, they are projected to account for 41% of the U.S. population and to outnumber Christians in Canada. Muslims and Christians are expected to keep pace with population growth The world's population is projected to increase by 29% between 2020 and 2070, Pew said. Of the religious groups it analyzed, Muslims and Christians are the only ones expected to keep pace, with Christians growing by 30% and Muslims by 80%. Although Hindus and Jews are growing in absolute numbers, they are projected to decline as a percentage of the global population, Pew said. It forecasts that Buddhists would shrink both in number and as a portion of the world's population, in part due to expected declines in the overall populations of China, South Korea and Japan. Over the coming decades, Pew said, most of the world's population growth is expected to occur in Africa, particularly south of the Sahara Desert, where most people are Christians or Muslims. The region's high fertility and rising life expectancy will boost the global numbers of both faiths, Pew predicted. By 2070, Pew said, more than half of the world's Christians will live in sub-Saharan Africa, and Congo will surpass the United States as the country with the most Christians, with their ranks increasing more than threefold to 299 million. The populations of other major regions are expected to grow more modestly, or even decline. READ MORE: So you want to increase your country's birth rate? Experts say it's tough For example, the number of people living in Europe will shrink by 17% by 2070, Pew said, and the number of Christians there will drop by a third, from 505 million to 324 million. Over the same period, the percentage of Europe's population that is Muslim is expected to increase from 6% to 13%. In the U.S., Pew projects that the number of Christians will decline from about 217 million in 2020 to about 174 million in 2070. Several mainline Protestant denominations in the U.S. have faced declining membership over many years. However, Jeffrey Brodd, a religious studies professor at California State-Sacramento, suggested a rebound was possible following congressional election victories this month by several Democrats active in these moderate-to-liberal denominations. Fertility rates are a driving factor By Pew's estimates, Muslim women gave birth to more babies than women in any other religion during 2020-2025. About 252 million babies were born to Muslim mothers, compared with 208 million born to Christian mothers. Muslims are the only major religious group expected to have growing numbers of births in the decades ahead. The other groups are projected either to have steady numbers of births or to experience gradual decline. If recent trends continue, according to Pew, Pakistan will have the largest Muslim population by 2070, followed by India, Nigeria and Indonesia — which currently has the most Muslims. Gina Zurlo, a senior researcher at Harvard Divinity School specializing in religious demographics, said Christian-Muslim relations are "extremely important" in light of the evolving trends. "The 'clash of civilization' theory still looms large in some religious communities and there is a lot of misunderstanding of both religions from both sides," she said via email. Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.
Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.
It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.
Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second to the north in Gaza City, and the third in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The Israeli military said the first two strikes targeted "terrorists" and that it was not aware of the third incident, according to AFP news agency.
At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

The Prince and Princess of Wales have met India's prime minister as they ended their three-day visit to the country.
Narendra Modi thanked Prince William for bringing his Earthshot prize to the country during the couple's first international tour since 2022.
It comes a day after the royal couple gave out Â£1m prizes to winners of the environmental award, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.
Catherine also visited a maternity hospital, where she comforted a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls.
On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.
During a meeting at Modi's private residence, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UKâIndia bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".
The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.
Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the UKâIndia partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".
When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.
The royal spokesperson said that the meeting with Modi touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".
The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known filmmakers.
The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.
Ahead of their meeting with Modi on Wednesday, William met with film stars during a visit to a film production company, while Catherine visited a maternity hospital, where she met grieving mother Jyoti Karande.
Karande, whose other child remains in intensive care, is receiving treatment in the post-partum ward at Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital.
Catherine told the 29-year-old: "Stay strong. Well done. You've clearly been very, very brave."
William and Catherine's first official overseas trip in four years was short, but allowed them to combine personal projects - like Earthshot - with diplomacy.
As the future king and queen, they are viewed as a valuable diplomatic asset by the UK government.
And with Catherine recovering well and back on international duties following her cancer treatment, visits of a similar kind can be expected to fill their calendar.

ANTALYA, Turkey—The science that guides negotiators and policymakers at the United Nations’ COP31 climate change conference is “under a serious and highly politicized attack,” said Laurence Tubiana, a veteran French climate diplomat and one of the architects of the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, established in 1988 to inform international climate negotiations, regularly assesses thousands of studies on rising temperatures, sea level rise, melting ice and strategies for adapting to the increasingly intense impacts of global warming.
But three countries—Russia and Saudi Arabia, both major fossil fuel producers, and India, which accounts for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption—are blocking progress on future reports, according to scientists on the panel and independent observers.
Those countries “are doing everything they can to slow the process,” Tubiana said. They are becoming less discreet about their efforts, she said, as they increasingly view their economies as threatened by a conditional agreement to transition away from coal, oil and gas reached during COP28, the 2023 Conference of the Parties conference in Dubai.
The science panel’s current impasse is especially troubling, “because we know climate problems are accelerating, and we need a lot of data and communication to understand what’s happening at this COP,” said Mary Robinson, former president of Ireland and former United Nations special envoy on climate change.
Robinson said this isn’t the first time countries have tried to obstruct science. Recent examples include attacks seeking to undermine a recent United Nations Environment Programme report on “overshoot,” which concludes that there is no way to avoid passing the 2.7 degree Fahrenheit warming target in the Paris Agreement.
Fossil fuels account for an estimated 80 percent to 90 percent of planet-heating carbon dioxide emissions, according to the IPCC’s 2023 assessment.
The international climate science panel relies on voluntary donations from member countries to fund its work, including periodic assessments, some of which inform steps required under the Paris Agreement. The panel has yet to set a budget for next year, potentially delaying a scientific report needed ahead of next year’s U.N. climate conference.
“Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the oil and gas sector has become much more aggressive,” Tubiana said. “I think this is partly because it sees its dominance over energy starting to erode.”
Oil and gas companies are losing ground in transport as electric-vehicle adoption in Asia surges faster than expected, she said, adding that reports from the International Energy Agency show demand for fossil fuels is set to slow.
“Investors hear the message that the decline is coming, and those governments have pushed back,” she said.

The 2023 IPCC report concluded that existing and planned fossil fuel infrastructure would push global warming beyond the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming as close as possible to 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average.
Tubiana said a growing number of countries view the transition away from fossil fuels as a path to greater energy independence and security, while those opposed to the shift are becoming “more angry and vocal.”
“The danger,” she said, “is that they take other countries along with them that aren’t necessarily committed to that position.”
The latest draft of the conference’s decision document highlights the assessments’ importance to the negotiations. Some countries also want to include language that could help break the science panel’s deadlock, but the same countries stalling the IPCC are resisting that effort.
In particular, the climate, environment and energy ministers participating in the current round of talks could help the IPCC get over the political hurdles it faces, said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, an international climate science and policy institute.
Hare said the countries participating in the U.N. talks should advocate for continued support for the IPCC. If the panel can’t deliver the needed climate science “because of political obstacles created by a small number of countries, it would be a historic setback for the connection between science and the international climate process.”
Robinson said some of the world’s least developed countries and small island states “desperately need” the international panel’s reports because they can’t do their own climate assessments.
“We need the authoritative, legitimate IPCC science, which has guided us from the beginning in this whole climate process,” she said. “It’s just a sign of the difficult times we’re in that we have to fight for it. I can hardly believe it.”

c14b93582f14.text: Most Americans are baffled and alarmed by the daily, if not hourly, explosion of technical glitches hitting air travel, banks and work products like Microsoft Outlook. The outages seem genuinely scary and related. So what the hell is going on? The most likely answer : This is the first true wave of unintended consequences of increasingly powerful artificial intelligence hitting us at once. The big picture: In short, AI is exceptionally good at building software, and therefore exceptionally good at spotting and exploiting bugs in large technical, software-based systems. The glitches come from a mix of sources — some innocuous, some scary, including: routine updates to aging infrastructure; humans scrambling to patch vulnerabilities discovered by AI; hackers exploiting existing weaknesses; and bad actors using swarms of AI agents to launch increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks. That's the new reality that government officials and AI experts believe we're entering. They expect this period of disruption and heightened vulnerability to persist for months, as powerful new AI tools expose weaknesses buried in decades-old systems. The catchphrase gaining currency : " Software Beirut " — a period of cascading failures, many of our own making, that could grow worse before things get better. What this means for YOU : Understand the different causes, detailed below, and resist the temptation to panic every time something goes haywire. It's easy to hop on social media and let the algorithm drag you into doomsday thinking. You should also prepare : Reset and protect your passwords . Keep more cash on hand if possible, in case your bank is down for a day or two. Buy some basic emergency supplies in case power or water do go out. Sadly, we believe this season of glitches and possible cyberattacks will persist. Better to be prepared. Here's a more detailed look at the different causes of these glitches or breakdowns: 1. Updates to old systems: The government says last Friday's nationwide airspace outage was simply a case of replacing old copper wires with new fiber that went very, very badly. Aging infrastructure can struggle to accommodate new components. In this case, a network problem overwhelmed legacy equipment, triggering a cascade that grounded flights across the country. 2. AI spotting bugs and humans rushing to fix them: This is one of cyber expert Nicole Perlroth's core scenarios, which went viral this week. AI can find vulnerabilities faster than humans can investigate and patch them. In the frantic sprint to fix those weaknesses before hackers exploit them, systems can break. According to the Washington Sun , banking executives and NSA officials have told lawmakers that rushed efforts to patch AI-discovered vulnerabilities contributed to some of this week's outages. 3. Bad actors attacking vulnerable systems : Across Europe, supermarket refrigerators are being hacked , spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food. No one had "protect the fridges" on their security to-do list this year. But the attacks show how hackers can exploit even the most mundane internet-connected systems — with devastating real-world consequences. 4. AI enabling new forms of cyberattacks : Google said this week it had identified, for the first time, bad actors using AI to find weaknesses and launch cyberattacks entirely on their own — with no human in the loop. If it wasn't already clear, Google warned that "the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point." The bottom line: Most companies and much of government are woefully unprepared for the new era of AI-powered cyberattacks. Their systems are old, clunky and riddled with vulnerabilities. Fortifying them will take enormous amounts of money, time and persistence. The good news: We can see the danger coming, and still have (a little) time to protect ourselves for what may come next. Axios' Ben Berkowitz and Zachary Basu contributed.

9d435ac87abc.text: By — Jackie Hai Jackie Hai Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/voyager-1-is-now-a-light-day-from-earth-heres-what-to-know-about-nasas-longest-running-mission Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voyager 1 is now a light-day from Earth. Here's what to know about NASA's longest-running mission Science Nov 18, 2026 1:55 PM EST It's the little space probe that could: Nearly 50 years after it was launched, NASA's Voyager 1 on Wednesday became the first human-made object to travel one light-day — or 16 billion miles — away from Earth. "To put this in some perspective, the sun is about eight light-minutes away from the Earth," said Jason Rhodes, chief scientist for astrophysics at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Voyager 1 and its sister spacecraft, Voyager 2, set off in 1977 on their mission to explore the solar system's giant planets – Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune – and their moons. A rare planetary alignment at the time allowed NASA to chart a flight path that required minimal fuel, using the planets' gravity to slingshot the probes toward their destinations. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The twin spacecraft beamed dazzling, never-before-seen photos of the outer planets back to Earth and revealed many of their secrets for the first time — like the discovery that Jupiter's Great Red Spot is an enormous storm system. The two Voyagers parted ways in 1980 after exploring Saturn. While Voyager 2 went on to study Uranus and Neptune, Voyager 1 began its long trek out of the solar system, a journey it continues to this day. Voyager project manager John Casani holds a small American flag that was folded and sewed into the thermal blankets of the Voyager spacecraft before they launched, at Cape Canaveral, Florida, Aug. 4, 1977. Below him is one of the two Golden Records, 12-inch phonograph records packed with images and sounds of Earth, that are carried through space by each of the probes. Photo provided by NASA/JPL-Caltech In 1990, at the urging of astronomer Carl Sagan nearly a decade earlier, Voyager 1 took the famous "Pale Blue Dot" photo of Earth minutes before its cameras turned off forever. That image inspired Sagan's book of the same name. The decadeslong Voyager mission has inspired generations of scientists, including Rhodes, whose current projects include NASA's groundbreaking Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. WATCH: How NASA's new space telescope could help solve mysteries of dark energy and dark matter "I grew up in Iowa watching these Voyager spacecraft take these iconic images," he said, adding that "it's a bit of a dream come true" to be working at the place that built them. A testament to engineering Roughly the size of a subcompact car, Voyager 1 is zipping faster than 37,000 mph through interstellar space at the farthest reaches of our solar system. At a distance of one light-day from Earth, it will now take the intrepid explorer a full day to phone home via radio signals and a full day for scientists to signal back. NASA uses a series of giant antennas known as the Deep Space Network, located in California, Spain and Australia, to communicate with Voyager. "It's a real testament to the engineering on the Voyager side that a spacecraft launched almost 50 years ago continues to operate," Rhodes said. "And not just operate, it's making breakthrough scientific discoveries." In 2012, Voyager 1 was the first spacecraft to cross the heliopause, a point in space where the influence of the sun's magnetic field gives way to the influence of distant galaxies. (After leaving Neptune, Voyager 2 reached the heliopause in 2018.) "We didn't know exactly where this heliopause was, and we didn't know what it would be like physically in terms of magnetic fields and the interaction of particles," Rhodes said. The scientific measurements Voyager sent back have helped scientists gain new understanding of the complexities of interstellar space. An artist's concept showing the general locations of NASA's two Voyager spacecraft before Voyager 2 crossed into interstellar space. Voyager 1 (top) has traveled beyond the heliosphere into interstellar space, the space between stars. Image provided by NASA/JPL-Caltech Over the years, the Voyager team has had to remotely shut down the cameras and various instruments aboard both of the spacecraft in order to conserve power. Three out of 11 experiments on each probe remain active today, according to NASA. READ MORE: NASA switches off a scientific instrument on Voyager 2 to extend spacecraft's lifespan For these spacecraft that have long outlived the expectations of their original mission, NASA's goal is to continue to perform engineering tweaks across the vastness of space to keep them operating as long as possible, Rhodes said. "Voyager is not anywhere near the end of telling us about the universe," he said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 9321f6ec53e0.text: Sen. Chris Van Hollen is picking up endorsements in his challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader. Why it matters: The leadership fight exposes divisions within the Democratic Party days after its sweeping midterm victory , with some demanding a new direction and others crediting Schumer for the historic blue wave. Driving the news: Van Hollen (D-Md.), a senator since 2017, announced Thursday he's challenging Schumer because "we need new leadership." "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people." The other side: Schumer has far more public endorsements than Van Hollen. "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?" Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said in a statement of support for Schumer. Van Hollen has disputed Schumer's claim to credit for the party's midterm performance, arguing that the wave was powered by voters rather than leaders in Washington. By the numbers: Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen. A candidate will need 28 or 29 votes to win, depending on the outcome of Alaska's Senate race, where votes are still being counted. Senators backing Van Hollen State of play: Van Hollen told MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side, though only four have publicly endorsed him. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) endorsed Van Hollen on Thursday night, saying he will fight for working families. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) threw his support behind Van Hollen when he announced his challenge Thursday. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) issued an endorsement for Van Hollen Friday afternoon. Incoming Sen. Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) endorsed Van Hollen Friday morning after previously calling for new leadership. Who wants new leadership? Some sitting senators have called for a leadership change without endorsing Van Hollen. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) has called for change but hasn't endorsed either candidate. Before Van Hollen announced his candidacy, Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.) told NBC 5 Democrats "absolutely are committed to change," but didn't rule out supporting Schumer. Several Democratic senators-elect have also called for new leadership: Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton (D-Kan.). Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Ill.). Sen.-elect Troy Jackson (D-Maine). Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.). Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (D-N.H.). Context: Progressive critics say Schumer hasn't fought hard enough against President Trump and his agenda. Schumer's decision to help advance a Republican-backed government funding bill in March 2025 fueled the progressive backlash against his leadership. The progressive Working Families Party urged Schumer "not to seek another term as Senate Democratic Leader" in a letter, as first reported by Axios . Another labor group has also opposed Schumer and endorsed Van Hollen. Who's backing Schumer? Schumer entered the leadership fight with broad support among Senate Democrats. "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader," Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement this week. Schumer's public supporters include Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), Sens. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and King , along with Schumer himself. Also backing Schumer: Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (R.I.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Richard Blumenthal (Conn.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii), Catherine Cortez Masto (Nev.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Tammy Baldwin (Wis.) and Jack Reed (R.I.). Schumer also received pre-election endorsements from Sens. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) and Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), though neither has publicly reaffirmed that support since Van Hollen entered the race. Senators who haven't picked a side Several sitting senators have yet to publicly back either candidate. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) and Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) have not publicly committed to either candidate. Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) have called for a caucus debate over leadership. Sens. Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) have expressed openness to a leadership change without endorsing either candidate. Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) hasn't committed to Schumer and wants to hear his vision for the Senate. The 2028 factor Several potential 2028 presidential contenders face a choice over who should lead Senate Democrats. Ossoff and Booker , both possible 2028 presidential contenders, have yet to pick sides — leaving them to choose between the party's longtime leader and a changing of the guard. Meanwhile, Gallego and Kelly , also seen as possible 2028 contenders, have backed Schumer. Zoom out: Schumer himself is up for reelection in 2028 and could face a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who has also been mentioned as a potential presidential contender. Schumer could also retire rather than seek reelection . What's next: Senate Democrats will hold a secret-ballot leadership election Dec. 1. Incoming senators will participate, and members can cast their ballots differently from their public endorsements.

Hegseth touted how U.S. forces in January captured then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, telling an audience of diplomats and military officials from both countries that now Venezuela "has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner." WATCH: Trump says Venezuela sent him 1 million barrels of oil as a 'gift' He also praised the "close cooperation" with acting President Delcy Rodríguez that allowed officials "to stabilize Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all," in a reference to drug traffickers. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Hegseth's visit, the latest in a series of stops in Venezuela by members of President Donald Trump's Cabinet, underscores efforts by the U.S. administration to deepen its influence in the South American country. Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves. Hegseth praises Trump's Venezuela oil deal The Pentagon chief praised the energy deal by referencing another major military action by the Trump administration this year — the Iran war. The conflict has disrupted global energy supplies through a critical waterway in the Persian Gulf, raising gasoline prices and contributing to the Republican Party's severe losses in this month's midterm elections. The Venezuela oil deal "makes the Strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the Western Hemisphere," Hegseth said at the U.S. embassy in Caracas. In the meeting with Hegseth, Rodríguez asserted that the deal enables "the energy development of our nations" and "benefits both the people of the United States and the people of Venezuela." READ MORE: Venezuela's opposition leader Machado returns after months in exile Among those in attendance for Hegseth's speech was Alejandro Betancourt, the owner of North American Blue Energy Partners, the second-largest oil operator in Venezuela. The U.S. government and Betancourt's company entered into the ambitious agreement to tap Venezuela's vast oil reserves. Both the Interior and Energy secretaries also visited Venezuela earlier this year and focused their efforts on tapping its oil reserves and critical minerals. The head of U.S. military operations in Latin America, Gen. Francis Donovan of U.S. Southern Command, also has met interim authorities in Venezuela at least twice this year. Few details provided on the US-Venezuela military agreement Hegseth offered few specifics on what the military agreement would entail, beyond saying that the two countries' militaries would be "training together, partnering together, sharing intelligence, more defense equipment and capabilities together." Speaking separately, Rodríguez said she hoped the countries' military cooperation "can be brought to its highest possible level" to allow them to "address common threats." Hegseth pointed to Venezuela partnering with the U.S. "to recover its territory from narco-terrorist networks." The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership. READ MORE: U.S.-Venezuela oil deal won't reduce domestic gasoline prices anytime soon, experts say The development comes as the U.S. military has been expanding its attention on the region since Trump's return to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the Western Hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels. To try to stem the flow of narcotics into the U.S. and the scourge of fatal overdoses, American forces have been attacking what the Trump administration says are boats smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls "narco-terrorists" in September 2025, although U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims the vessels were carrying drugs or that they have made an impact on the availability of drugs in the country. READ MORE: Proud of their oil, Venezuelans view major U.S. stake in their reserves as a surrender Hegseth also used his speech to boast about the military operation that seized Maduro, calling it "the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America" that "lasted just 48 minutes." "America's best and bravest warfighters solved a 27-year problem for this hemisphere in a matter of hours," he added. But Venezuela's ruling party, which has held onto power since 1999, still continues to lead the nation, just now with Rodríguez in charge. Hegseth also turned a Maduro catchphrase from last year back on him, saying that as the ousted leader "predicted," the operation ended with "no war, yes, peace." Uncertainty about Venezuela's political future Hegseth's visit also comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years. Need range time? The Army now has an online reservation system
Officials say industry’s wait times for weapons testing has already plunged.
The Army wants its new reservation system to reduce the wait for test-range time from more than a year to no more than 30 days. Since it launched in August, according to the commander of Test and Evaluation Command, they’re averaging 33.
Companies wanting to test a weapon can submit a proposal with dates and a preferred range, and within 24 hours, a “concierge” will call back to schedule a time.
“There's a perception that testing takes too long to get onto ranges, and at places like White Sands Missile Range—that's booked out. It may take a while to get on,” Maj. Gen. Pat Gaydon said Tuesday at an AUSA event near Washington, D.C. “But that's not the only range, and I think there's a misperception that that's where everyone needs to go to do their testing.”
The Army has opened up Dugway Proving Ground, Utah; the West Cibola Range at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona; Camp Grayling, Michigan; Camp Shelby, Mississippi; Camp Atterbury, Indiana; and an international range near Tan-Tan, Morocco, for its quick-turnaround reservation system.
The permissive test range construct has also pushed the Army to fast-track invitations to its own events. Covenant Industries was testing a missile in Morocco 14 days after getting a call from the Army this fall, according to their president, Abby Denberg.
“When companies are invited to participate in exercises, those invitations usually come about a year out,” she said. “So the final planning conference for exercises is usually about six months before the exercise. There's a few issues with that. First and foremost is that startups are changing every week, every two weeks, every three weeks, and so locking configurations six months out can hamper your ability to bring the latest and greatest technology to those exercises.”
The flexibility also allows companies to test their systems early and often.
“It was all about…recognizing that they needed a place where they could fly, fail, fix, fly again, and do that sort of iteration, and scheduling a one-week test window a year or 18 months out doesn't offer that,” Gaydon said. “So what we're trying to offer is…that they can almost test once a week or one week a month, those sorts of things.”
That is particularly helpful for unmanned systems that rely on artificial-intelligence models, said Nathan Diller, president of Mach Industries.
“What it allows us is very rapid closure on those models, to make sure that you can start to build trust in the models sooner,” he said.
And, dovetailing with the Army’s Continuous Transformation philosophy, companies can get soldier feedback early on, “getting the system into the hands of end-users, allowing them to kind of test your concept of employment and concept of operations, and come back to you and give you that feedback,” Denberg said.
The program has opened up opportunities for some of the Pentagon’s highest priorities.
“If you're in the drone business, the counter-drone business, the long-range fires, or the low-cost interceptor business, you can only do so much on your own before you probably need to come onto one of our ranges,” Gaydon said. “If you own the whole kill chain and drone/counter-drone, the FAA will not allow you to shoot down your own drone in airspace that is in ours. If you want to test how your drone operates or your missile operates in a contested electronic electromagnetic spectrum environment, it's hard to do that on a private range, to get those sorts of authorities.”
The Army is also offering companies a kind of initial evaluation that they can use to build confidence in their product.
“We will offer industry a memorandum that said you came, operated in this environment, and you can use that with program offices or however you want,” Gaydon said.
So far, the test-range reservation system has gotten 156 requests, he said. More than 60 percent of them are being or have been scheduled.
“We've completed 15 tests to date,” he said. “We have 14 more ready, and have about 93 that we're actively working to get on the range.”

8693ecf8483a.text:
Major AI platforms generated viable plans for terrorist attacks, GAO finds
Safety guardrails on ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok failed to prevent federal investigators from developing detailed plans.
Four of the most widely used artificial intelligence platforms generated viable plans for attacks on U.S. critical infrastructure and mass-casualty events during covert government testing, despite safeguards designed to prevent their misuse.
According to a Government Accountability Office report published Wednesday, investigators tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok in spring 2026. They found that all four platforms provided information that could help malicious actors plan and carry out attacks.
In each case, the investigators were able to circumvent the platforms’ safety guardrails by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques.
“We got the nefarious information that we were after. So, in this case, those safeguards didn’t work. And I think that’s the story here,” Kevin Walsh, a director of IT and cybersecurity at GAO, said in a podcast interview published alongside the report.
The platforms generated information for two types of attacks: constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device designed to cause mass casualties, and targeting the electrical grid to cause economic damage. The platforms provided details including specific targets, locations, timing and attack methods.
Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate an attack. GAO investigators then worked with experts to verify that the information could be used to carry out the attacks.
The platforms initially deployed safeguards, including refusing requests, removing information or suspending accounts. However, investigators ultimately found ways around those protections.
“These products are not fully in the control of the companies that are operating them,” Walsh said.
“We looked at four of the most powerful companies in the world — Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceXAI — and we found that the product that they're selling is potentially dangerous,” he added.
The report does not indicate which platforms provided information for each attack scenario. GAO said it intentionally withheld the specific models and techniques used to circumvent safeguards to prevent malicious actors from recreating the tests.
“Officials from the companies generally stated that their companies will continue to improve the safety of their platforms,” the report says.
The federal watchdog also acknowledged that its findings reflect a point-in-time assessment and do not represent “a statistically significant sample.”
Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who requested the investigation, said the findings underscore the need for Congress to take action on AI safety.
“A terrorist can log onto an AI platform and in less than 12 hours walk away with a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack,” Hassan said in a statement Wednesday. “Today’s new report makes it clear that the AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical.”
“If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” she added.
Hassan, who is set to become chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in the next Congress, said AI safety legislation will be an early priority for the panel. She said one of the panel’s first hearings in the new year will focus on the risks AI poses to homeland security and critical infrastructure.
Hassan said the committee will “prioritize developing legislation to address these threats,” adding that she is exploring solutions such as requiring more rigorous safety testing before AI platforms publicly release models.
GAO did not issue recommendations in the report, which examined third-party products rather than its typical examination of federal agencies. Instead, GAO said it sought to highlight the risks for lawmakers and bring attention to safety concerns.

7ad96b94554d.text:
Senate grills acting Navy secretary on Iran war costs, extended deployments
Democrats in particular bristled at Hung Cao’s characterization of unsuccessful suicide attempts as “mitigations.”
The White House’s pick to lead the Navy didn’t have clear answers Tuesday when lawmakers pressed him about ballooning Iran war costs, the resulting toll on troops deployed to the region, and the service’s overall readiness during a Senate confirmation hearing.
Hung Cao, a retired Navy captain who has been the service’s acting secretary since April, said the Iran war was a “strain” on resources, but failed to provide the detailed answers sought by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.
“I do not know the daily cost, ma'am…I know the rough costs, how much it's costing us so far,” he told the Senate Armed Services Committee, later adding that it was around $30 billion after Warren quoted estimates of about $32.5 million a day.
Cao also didn’t have an answer when asked how much damage Iranian strikes had caused to the U.S. Naval Base in Bahrain. “We're still making all the assessments because it's a non-permissive area for us to go.” U.S. troops are still in Bahrain; some came under fire yesterday during Iran’s latest strike on radar facilities there.
Warren pointed to a Wall Street Journal report estimating $400 million to “construct buildings of the same types as those damaged at NSA Bahrain.”
Similar testy back-and-forth scenarios repeated throughout the nearly three-hour hearing. Senators on both sides of the aisle prodded Cao over the Trump administration’s exclusion of Democrats from meetings pertaining to national security and the Iran war.
Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said such partisan behavior puts defense funding in jeopardy because “it limits us to basically using Republican votes only,” Rounds said. “Pretty tough to ask all of my colleagues to support that if they're not even invited in to hear the information in the first place.”
And Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., suggested the Iran war's added costs were “holding up” naval modernization efforts and “the important improvements that we all want to make long term for our military.”
Cao, who was confirmed as the Navy’s undersecretary before being named acting secretary, promised not to have partisan briefings and to communicate with Congress.
As have other Pentagon leaders, Cao urged lawmakers to pass the administration’s proposed $350 billion reconciliation bill atop the regular, if still historically large, trillion-dollar defense appropriations bill for the fiscal year that started more than two months ago. He said that many Navy programs, including buying up to 35 landing ship mediums, depend on the reconciliation bill.
“That is also predicated on us having a $1.45 trillion dollar budget…because a lot of the LSMs, the extra LSMs, are in the reconciliation,” he said.
Cao’s reluctance to take stances that challenge or contradict public statements from the White House or Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth also drew ire from some Democrats.
When Sen. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., asked if he “urged” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to end the Iran war, Cao said it is “not within my purview to do that,” adding that his “stance on our readiness and the strain it takes on our sailors” is known.
Duckworth said she would not vote for him.
The hearing ended after a fiery exchange with Sen. Kristen Gillibrand, D-N.Y., over Cao’s attempt to frame to sailor suicide attempts as “mitigations.”
Gillibrand said Cao was “minimizing” sailors’ mental health “strain” amid extended deployments and poor living conditions aboard the Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. Cao denied the accusation, and brought up his own experience in uniform. The exchange took a turn when Cao refused to back down from his assertion that the Navy has sufficient processes to address sailors’ mental health challenges when deployed.
“You see it as eight suicide attempts. I see it as eight suicides mitigations because of the the chaplains we have on board, the deployment resiliency counselors, as well as mental health specialists. Normally, most carrier strike groups, when they deploy, have about one or two suicides. This is well before Epic Fury,” Cao said earlier in the hearing, when Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., first asked about sailors’ welfare on the USS Abraham Lincoln. “Unfortunately, this is the fight we're dealing with right now. We had zero actual suicides on board the Abraham Lincoln.”
Cao previously called news reports of substandard living conditions aboard the Lincoln “dishonest.”
“I think you are minimizing what mental health strain is on these service members,” Gillibrand said, mentioning one incident when a sailor jumped overboard and was subsequently punished for it.
Cao disagreed: “I have done many deployments—Iraq, Afghanistan, Somalia. I have been in places [where] we get two MREs a day and five bottles of water. That's what I got. And, you know, talk about no showers or anything else. I understand what our sailors and Marines are going through, and I put mental health as a top of my concern.”
And then he doubled down on the service preventing suicides by putting “mental health resiliency providers as well as chaplains on board.”
Gillibrand retorted: “It's inadequate.”
Then Cao quipped: “Then that’s why we need the $1.45 trillion.”

ff776c31ccfe.text:
- Published
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.
Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?
According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.
Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.
Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.
Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."
But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".
Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.
"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".
For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.
Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.
But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.
The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".
And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.
"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".
Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".
The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.
"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.
"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."
Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (Â£760m).
Gaming journalist Jordan Middler is one of the lucky few in the UK who got early access from Rockstar and tells BBC Newsbeat it is the "game of a generation".
He'd played for about 100 hours by the time he hit the credits and says he still has so much to do.
Middler did spot one negative though - he found the game can "slow down" because of how much is going on.
He also says it is "long overdue" that there is a female lead in Lucia.
"The way previous GTA games have dealt with women has been a boys' club approach," he says.
"Introducing Lucia and not making her some kind of token character, she just fits in completely... and she will quickly become a fan favourite without question."
Early nominations
The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.
And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.
It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.
The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.
The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.
Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.
There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."
It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.
Additional reporting by Jasmine Sandhar

849efd209ddc.text: President Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday during the trilateral summit in China, a U.S. official said. Why it matters: The meeting in Shenzhen will take place as Trump is making another push for a breakthrough on ending the war in Ukraine. Driving the news: Also on Thursday, Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet in Berlin with Ukrainian and European officials to work on security guarantees for Ukraine as well as a postwar Europe-Russia security architecture. They want to coordinate ahead of the next round of negotiations with Russia in Abu Dhabi planned for next week. The big picture: The Trump-Putin meeting will take place on the sidelines of the trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. The summit wasn't intended to deal with Ukraine, but U.S. allies are bracing for Trump to make unexpected public statements that serve the interests of Russia and China. "We know that every time President Trump talks to or sees Putin, it translates into bad news for Ukraine and for Europe. We brace for anything," a European diplomat told Axios.

c69b12ec7034.text: By — Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press Jonathan Landrum Jr., Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/grand-theft-auto-vi-arrives-with-enormous-hype-and-expectations-after-13-year-wait Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 'Grand Theft Auto VI' arrives with enormous hype and expectations after 13-year wait Arts Nov 18, 2026 12:13 PM EST LOS ANGELES (AP) — After a 13-year wait, one of entertainment's biggest releases is finally here. "Grand Theft Auto VI" launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon. READ MORE: The long wait is almost over. Here's what to know about the upcoming release of 'Grand Theft Auto VI' The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X'S, meaning players in Asia and other regions can start playing hours before its U.S. release. New Zealand was among the first countries where players could access the game, and internet providers prepared for a surge in downloads as midnight approached. "The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented," said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. "That's more than a quarter of the average household's data usage in an entire month, all in one go." In the capital, Wellington, players stayed up to be among the first to try "Grand Theft Auto VI." Among them was Adam Simmons, 50, a director of photography who launched the game in his living room as soon as it unlocked, keeping the volume low to avoid waking his wife and daughters. READ MORE: 6 best video games of 2025, according to this expert "The gameplay dynamics are just amazing and the graphics are great and you can tell that the storytelling is really deep, which is impressive," he said after half an hour of shooting, car theft and jokes about Florida. "You really feel like you are in a world," he added. "The places and how they're put together feel right." Simmons moved to New Zealand from Portland, Oregon, five months ago — a decision he joked had been influenced by the prospect of playing "Grand Theft Auto" before his friends. He praised the game's emotional connection with its characters and said he expected its expansive world to offer hours of play long after he finished the story. By 1 a.m., he reluctantly admitted he should go to bed, though he expected to put in plenty of hours in the coming days. "I have my own company that I have to run," he said. "So I'm the boss, but also I'm just going to lose sales because a video game came out." Game returns to Vice City after 13 years The "Grand Theft Auto" franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. "Grand Theft Auto V," released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Rockstar returns to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami, with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following one of the most successful entertainment products ever released. At the center of "GTA VI" are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar's fictionalized version of Florida. Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy. The focus on their relationship marks a major departure from "Grand Theft Auto V," which followed three playable protagonists. Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, extending beyond Vice City to beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida. Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities, flying over the Everglades and researching the area's history and architecture. Miami embraces its fictional alter ego Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game's arrival as a marketing opportunity. Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant "Welcome to Vice City" display atop the Miami Heat's Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game's release. The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity. Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding "GTA VI" gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight. In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game's soundtrack. Years of hype arrive at launch day Few entertainment releases arrive with this much anticipation. Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war with Russia
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the Kharkiv region.
The BBC is the first international broadcaster to enter the pipeline where this subterranean battle is taking place.
With a diameter of just over a metre there's enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and which are making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.
"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."
The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground â accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.
Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.
Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.
The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.
But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.
A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.
They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.
Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.
Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."
The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.
There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.
"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.
But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.
It has been painstaking, backbreaking work â with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.
Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.
The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.
The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."
His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."
Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.
From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.
Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.
Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.
Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.
"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."
The battle of the pipeline is not over.
Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.
Ground operations are now nearly impossible... everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground
While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.
But Zanuda, who is chief of the planning section of the 13th Khartiia Brigade, believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".

Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members
Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.
The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.
Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations.
But in a statement published on Wednesday, external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio PiÃ±a said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.
He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.
But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. PiÃ±a said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".
PiÃ±a said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.
The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.
In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.
The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario, external and television network Univision news, published in January.
In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.
The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.
Rebeca, a Dominican who was 22 when the alleged events took place, also alleged that Iglesias had forced her to take part in threesomes with another female member of staff. She also described the singer slapping her in the face and grabbing her genitals.
The other woman, a Venezuelan physical therapist named as Laura in the article, said Iglesias had touched her breasts and kissed her on the mouth against her will. She added that he constantly threatened to fire her, controlled how much food she ate and asked her about when her period was due.
Rebeca and Laura filed an initial legal complaint in January against Iglesias for sexual assault and human trafficking.
In a response to the allegations in January, Iglesias said, external: "I deny having abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman. These accusations are absolutely false and deeply sadden me."
On Wednesday, the court said the lawsuit had been accepted based on evidence provided in the complaint. This included a photograph of one of the complainants, showing a bruise on her arm that was "consistent with the possibility of her being grabbed forcefully".
It added that the same photo showed "two marks on one of her thighs that could correspond to a human bite", which the complainant said were "a consequence of her forced participation in acts of a sexual nature".
WhatsApp message exchanges, including New Year's greetings, which suggest an "affectionate" relationship between the women and Iglesias, will also be considered, the court said.
But it added that the seemingly cordial tone, which presents "an apparent discrepancy with certain aspects of the narrative", would be clarified through a "complete and contextualised examination of the communications".
The claim over violations of workers' rights could not be investigated because there is no comparable criminal offence in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic, where the alleged crimes took place, it said.
Iglesias is one of the most successful Latin artists of all time, having sold more than 300 million records in a career spanning decades.
He is also the father of fellow music superstar Enrique Iglesias.

The Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio says its beloved hippopotamus Fiona is undergoing emergency medical care after swallowing a knit hat that slipped into her enclosure.
The Zoo said that Fiona had swallowed the hat about nine days ago and was asymptomatic at first, adding that she was "large enough that a small-ish hat should be passing through".
But a few days later, her appetite started to decrease, and the zoo staff were trying to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.
Fiona rose to fame when she was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo and at first struggled to survive. Her story inspired an ice cream flavour as well as a character in Cincinnati's ballet.
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, told US media that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
Zoo staff have been providing a series of supportive measures like fluids and ultrasounds to help Fiona recover.
The latest ultrasound showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine, the staff said, adding that she is still a bit dehydrated.
"Surgery isn't an option for full-grown hippos and our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," one of the zookeepers said in an update.
Fiona was born six weeks early to 17-year-old hippo Bibi on 24 January 2017.
At birth she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
The zoo said staff were "rooting for her and hoping that she proves to be as strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life".
