‘I was seriously wrong’: Experts say superintelligent AI may arrive as soon as next year
AI is speeding up research, potentially creating a runaway loop.
Some forecasters who closely track AI developments have drastically revised predictions this month, saying that “artificial superintelligence” may arrive years earlier than they thought.
Sentinel, a forecasting group, now expects superhuman AI to arrive around 2028, not 2031. The AI Futures Project, which last year laid out a scenario in which superintelligent AI might arrive in 2027, says development is proceeding faster than the scenario assumed.
Both groups changed their predictions in response to a Nov. 5 report by METR, a nonprofit that evaluates AI risks. METR found that the speed at which AI models were improving within AI developer Anthropic had roughly doubled since late last year, which it attributed mostly to the extensive use of AI agents to help with research.
Some experts think AI-driven research could start a runaway loop of AI improving itself, known as recursive self-improvement, a threat they say demands quick action.
“Long, deliberate processes are not going to cut it for the pace at which this is moving,” said Joe O’Brien, a researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, a think tank. “This is something that is going to have to be addressed under the current administration, with the incoming Congress. And quickly.”
‘A big update’
To groups that monitor the progress of AI development, the METR report arrived like a bomb.
“This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected,” the AI Futures Project wrote in a Nov. 10 update, adding that AI researchers better than the best human expert will “likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown).”
“I was seriously wrong,” wrote METR researcher Ryan Greenblatt, who was not involved in the report, Nov. 5 on X. “This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI [artificial superintelligence] within 1-2 years.”
Not everyone is convinced. Ramez Naam, a computer scientist and futurist who founded the venture capital firm PlanetaryVC, wrote on X that METR’s conclusions are too hard to verify.
“The METR report on progress at Anthropic is missing too much,” Naam wrote. “I completely trust the METR team to go into this with integrity. But we all have different priors and sometimes pull very different conclusions out of the same data.”
The terms of the report’s publication gave METR access to Anthropic’s internal data, but allowed Anthropic to redact any of that data from the public report. This included removing what METR called “a majority of the evidence we found most informative.”
“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” wrote Sam McCandlish, an Anthropic co-founder, on X. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster. That would make the risks METR is worried about worse. That’s a tradeoff. I think we made the right call, though we’re continuing to assess the pros and cons here.”
Officials with Anthropic, which raised $81 billion today in a record-breaking initial public offering, did not respond to a request for comment.
METR declined to comment.
Still, some of the leading figures in AI say that, missing data or not, this time is different.
Four days after the METR report came out, Paul Christiano delivered the opening Hinton Lecture in Toronto, where Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, one of the “godfathers of AI,” introduced him as “one of the most important researchers working on AI safety.” Christiano is a former head of safety at the federal Center for AI Standards and Innovation and AI Safety Institute, and helped develop reinforcement learning from human feedback, a widely used technique in today’s AI models, while a researcher at OpenAI.
In his address, Christiano delivered a stark warning.
“I think there is a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years,” he said, because AI is speeding up research. “We are seeing what you might expect to see at the beginning of a process of acceleration, or shortly before you saw 10 years of progress compressed into a short period of time,” he said.
Christiano predicted that the AI system that emerges from this process would surpass human skills in many, perhaps most, of the areas where current systems are weak. He said such an AI could control drones and construction robots, giving it both military hardware and the ability to build infrastructure without human help, or use its hacking skills to spread to servers around the world, preventing attempts to simply “pull the plug.”
Today’s much less capable AI has already found vulnerabilities in every major operating system and web browser.
If the pace of AI progress keeps accelerating, “Congress, the U.S. government, and humanity more generally, will probably end up completely disempowered by around the end of 2027. Or maybe early 2028,” said Daniel Kokotajlo, executive director of the AI Futures Project and a former researcher at OpenAI.
Policy and politics
More than 1,300 AI company employees have signed a statement about the need to slow the pace of AI development and negotiate with China to slow as well. Congress and public opinion suggest a shift toward support for regulation.
But the White House has resisted pressure to more closely regulate domestic AI, instead rebranding AI as “Super Intelligence” as part of an effort to boost public support for the technology. On Friday, the Pentagon renamed its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office the Super Intelligence Office. “As the Super Intelligence Office our mission is to harness the full power of sovereign Super Intelligence to ensure decisive military superiority across every domain,” the office said in a press release. It declined to comment fur

European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders - Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron - were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials haven't budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.
As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.

39abb61454f2.text: By — Patrick Aftoora Orsagos, Associated Press Patrick Aftoora Orsagos, Associated Press By — John Seewer, Associated Press John Seewer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/cincinnati-zoo-says-fiona-the-hippo-has-died-more-than-a-week-after-ingesting-a-hat Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Cincinnati Zoo says Fiona the hippo has died, more than a week after ingesting a hat Nation Nov 19, 2026 4:11 PM EST CINCINNATI (AP) — Fiona, the hippo whose premature birth and fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation nearly a decade ago, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure more than a week ago. "It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency," the zoo said in a statement. The zoo said Monday that Fiona was undergoing care around the clock after swallowing the hat more than a week ago. Before she died, veterinarians had been keeping Fiona hydrated, giving her treats and monitoring her every move, the zoo said. They even borrowed a vibration plate from a horse farm, encouraging her to stand on it several times a day in the hopes that the shaking would help move things along through her digestive tract. READ MORE: Gramma the Galapagos tortoise, oldest resident of San Diego Zoo who delighted visitors for almost a century, dies at about 141 Grace Brooks, of Cincinnati, and her two children, ages 3 and 5, had Fiona on their minds when they arrived at the zoo Thursday, before her death was announced. Her kids have been talking about Fiona at preschool, she said. "They said she needed to poop, which is, you know, true," Brooks said with a laugh. "They know all about Fiona, and we have lots of books about her." The zoo was mostly empty, though a small crowd was gathered inside the "Hippo Cove," where two other hippos were swimming. Even without Fiona in the cove, her presence was felt. There's a holiday-themed Fiona statue just outside the entrance, and the gift shop has an entire wall filled with hippo-themed shirts, coffee mugs, shot glasses and books, including "A Very Fiona Christmas" and "You've Got This, Fiona." Fiona was under close care Fiona captivated people worldwide after her premature birth in 2017. She swallowed the hat about 11 days ago after a zoo visitor tossed it in the air. A ceiling fan caught and catapulted the hat through a small opening above the area's viewing windows. It was an accident, said zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley. Before she died, Mike Wenninger, the zoo's director of animal health, said veterinarians had sedated her twice to evaluate her condition. An ultrasound on Tuesday showed some bunching of her intestines, indicating she was still trying to pass the obstruction, Wenninger said. They also conducted a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope, but were unable to detect anything, he said. "Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked," Curley said Wednesday in the latest update on Fiona's condition. "And they were happy to see her respond." Surgery would be challenging Specialists told the zoo that surgery wasn't an option for full-grown hippos, the zoo said. Hippos have a digestive system that would make Fiona's situation tricky, Jack Kottwitz, an assistant professor at Michigan State University's College of Veterinary Medicine, said before her death was announced. "They have a multichambered stomach for digesting plants — sort of like a cow — but they don't regurgitate and chew cud like a cow does. Those multiple chambers, tissue folds, fluid, and digesting food easily 'hide' the hat, making removal with an endoscope from the stomach chambers very difficult," Kottwitz told The Associated Press in an email. Surgery is a major logistical challenge for many reasons, he said. In order to find the hat, multiple incisions might be needed during a very long surgery, he said. But hippos are notoriously difficult to anesthetize and have skin over 2 inches (5 centimeters) thick in places. Hippos also really need access to water, and Fiona would have to be kept out of the water for several days post-surgery to allow any incisions to heal, he said. "Because there is no reliable way to pinpoint whether the hat is in the stomach, intestine, or colon, surgeons may have to carefully explore the entire digestive tract — stomach, intestine and colon — to find it," Kottwitz said. Jan Hawkins, doctor of veterinary medicine at North Carolina State University, said Fiona's situation was difficult because it was hard to tell exactly where the hat was. "You just don't know because you can't do the normal imaging and things that you can do in some of the smaller animals, or even horses," Hawkins said. Other zoo animals have also died from eating foreign objects Zoos around the world have warned for years about the dangers posed by objects that are tossed or blown into animal habitats. Two years ago, a rare antelope choked to death after eating the plastic lid from a squeezable fruit pouch at a zoo in Tennessee. A polar bear at a German zoo died in 2014 after swallowing a jacket dropped into his enclosure by a visitor. Veterinarians say a common reason for pet owners to make emergency visits is after their dogs have swallowed balls, toys and strings. Fiona became a sensation after Harambe's death Fiona survived her first health scare when she was born six weeks premature. She weighed just 29 pounds (13.2 kilograms), which was less than the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at that time. Fiona was unable to nurse, so a zoo staffer hand-milked her mother. Already, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have raised concerns over the risks, including the potential for advanced AI models to be abused and the additional volatility such IPOs could introduce into the financial system.

Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) said "a lot of people would be able to guess" if she regrets voting to confirm the embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, during Axios' Future of Defense Summit Thursday. Why it matters: The retiring Iowa senator, who served in the military for more than two decades, has been notably skeptical of Hegseth, and hasn't always been in lockstep with the Trump administration. Catch up quick: Despite her hesitancy over his nomination, Ernst ultimately voted to confirm Hegseth . However, she's continued to question him throughout his tenure. She recently questioned whether the embattled Pentagon leader has been "truthful" about the status of the Iran war, which she said Iowans rejected in the midterms. "If there is deception coming from our Pentagon and being transmitted to the president, I would want to know that," Ernst told reporters earlier this month. Driving the news: "There is very little transparency right now with what is being discussed between the White House and the Department of War," Ernst said of Pentagon communication over the war in Iran in a conversation with Axios' defense and space reporter Thomas Novelly. "As Congress, we would expect that we would be read into some of those conversations, and unfortunately, we have not been read into those conversations," she added. State of play: Ernst sits on the Senate Committee on Armed Services, where she chairs the Emerging Threats and Capabilities subcommittee. She predicted in her interview with Novelly that given the "not even hidden animosity" between Democrats and Hegseth, "it will be very difficult" for new Senate Armed Services Committee leadership to receive information. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

Following a week of flight delays, website outages and the possibility of an Iranian dirty bomb attack, House lawmakers grilled top administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, about threats to the United States. WATCH: Lawmakers press Mullin on flight disruptions and ICE tactics Mullin, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee that the outages affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, the National Security Agency and private companies such as Chase, Apple and United Airlines were unrelated and not the result of hostile cyberattacks. "Based on what we know today … these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes," Clayton told the committee Nov. 18. While stopping short of blaming artificial intelligence-driven cyberdefense upgrades for the outages, Clayton said AI "is reshaping the cybersecurity landscape. It is sharply increasing speed, scale and sophistication of offensive and defensive cyber operations." Hours after flights were cleared to resume on Nov. 13, Mullin was in the air, bound for a football game. He defended his decision to the committee to take a government plane to the Louisiana State University vs. Texas game following the nationwide ground stop, saying he was keeping a promise to his family and wanted his trip to temper public fears about whether it was safe to fly. At the time of his flight, hundreds of thousands of passengers were still grappling with logistical challenges from more than 9,000 canceled flights and 7,000 delays the day before, according to the tracking service FlightAware. Here are a few other highlights from the hearing, fact-checked. Did Mullin vote against more FAA funding while in Congress? U.S. Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., put a spotlight on Mullin's FAA funding votes while he was serving in Congress. "You and (Transportation) Secretary (Sean) Duffy criticized Congress for failing to prioritize investments in our nation's aging air traffic control infrastructure. But in 2021, Congress passed the bipartisan infrastructure law providing $25 billion for aviation infrastructure, including $5 billion specifically for FAA facilities and equipment," McIver said. "How did you vote on that legislation? … I'll tell you how you voted. You voted against it." Mullin did oppose that bill, but he voted for FAA funding other times. WATCH: Mullin defends Trump administration's messaging on spate of outages, flight to football game during ground stop In November 2021, while representing Oklahoma's 2nd House District, Mullin and a majority of House Republicans voted against President Joe Biden's bipartisan infrastructure bill. The legislation authorized $1.2 trillion in total spending and included $25 billion for aviation overall, with $5 billion for FAA facilities and equipment, including air traffic control centers and aging infrastructure. Republican support for the bill was critical to its passage, with 13 Republicans voting for it in the House, and 19 in the Senate. The Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2021 that the legislation could add $256 billion to the deficit over 10 years. Republicans who opposed the bill, including Mullin, cited the cost and said plans to offset it weren't robust enough. "Only $110 billion of this package will go towards improving actual infrastructure, like roads and bridges, and Oklahoma would only receive a small fraction of that money," Mullin said in a news release at the time. At other times in his House career, Mullin voted for other aviation funding bills, such as the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, the Disaster Tax Relief and Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2017 and the bipartisan FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018. As a U.S. senator, Mullin voted for the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, which authorized $17.8 billion for FAA facilities and equipment through fiscal year 2028. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., accused the Trump administration of firing federal workers who handle cybersecurity threats, singling out DHS and the FBI. The agencies "have decimated the cybersecurity personnel that this administration entered office with," Goldman said. "(The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) is way down because the president didn't want election fraud to be uncovered. The FBI has fired numerous cybersecurity agents because they may or may not have served a subpoena in the Mar-a-Lago case." This is partially accurate. 9282bf1d5b76.text: Major grocery retailers are switching up their Thanksgiving dinner deals this year, with a few lowering prices, others swapping out items and some shifting toward more flexible meal options. The big picture: Lower advertised prices from some retailers could offer relief to Americans already stretching their holiday budgets , but shifting menus mean shoppers may not be getting the same bang for their buck. State of play: Higher fuel costs, poor growing conditions and other inflationary pressures have pushed up food prices ahead of the holiday. The American Farm Bureau Federation said the cost of an average Thanksgiving feast for ten has increased 6% since 2025, totaling an estimated $58.63. The increase is largely driven by price hikes for turkey, milk, rolls and cranberries, the federation said. Driving the news: Walmart is advertising a lower price for its Thanksgiving meal than in 2025, while offering 18% more individual items. The retailer said this year's meal , which serves ten people for $35, is its "lowest priced one-click basket" ever, down from $39.93 last year. The complete meal comes with a turkey, multiple sides and pumpkin pie to finish. It adds ingredients for sweet potato casserole and corn muffins, but drops macaroni and cheese and baby carrots from last year's spread. Fried onions were the only item to switch from name-brand to store-brand in 2026. The other side: Aldi is also promoting a Thanksgiving meal $1 cheaper than in 2025, though several dishes have changed . Instead of a 14-pound turkey, the 2026 dinner will have a 16-pound bird. It includes several sides, but not fan favorites such as mashed potatoes and gravy, macaroni and cheese or green bean casserole. Zoom out: Costco's gourmet Thanksgiving dinner is more elaborate than its cook-at-home grocery counterparts, with a similar menu and the same advertised promotional price as last year. Both 2025 and 2026 dinners cost $199.99, serve eight people and include a five-pound turkey breast. The prepared meal includes the same traditional sides and desserts, with the addition of candied yams. This year's dinner is marketed as 30 pounds, compared with 28 pounds in some descriptions of last year's offerings. The intrigue: Kroger is shifting away from the fixed-price "Freshgiving" Thanksgiving meal bundle it offered in previous years. Instead, it is promoting individual holiday discounts and prepared foods in various portion sizes. Kroger's chief marketing officer said the approach is intended to make holiday meals more convenient and accommodate gatherings of different sizes. In 2025, Kroger advertised a Thanksgiving meal for 10 for under $4.75 a person, providing a 14- to 16-pound frozen turkey and traditional sides. The bottom line: Your food preferences, guest count and budget will help determine if a Thanksgiving meal deal is the right choice for you. Go deeper: Wholesale food prices are on the rise

Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.
Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The case brought by The Gambia centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
After fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (Arsa) launched deadly attacks on more than 30 police posts there, Myanmar troops, backed by local Buddhist mobs, launched a wave of violence, prompting a mass exodus of Rohingya.
Refugees recounted entire villages being burned down and the mass killing of civilians, while numerous survivors and eyewitnesses provided testimony that the Myanmar military had also raped and abused Rohingya women and girls.
The ICJ determined that around 10,000 Rohingya were "violently killed" during the clearance operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
Iwasawa said Myanmar's military engaged in "indiscriminate" killings, the execution of men, "widespread" sexual violence, "extreme violence" against children and the deliberate burning of Rohingya homes.
He said the military had also attacked Rohingya as they were fleeing to Bangladesh.
Myanmar, he added, had engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" by burning or disposing of bodies, burned and bulldozed sites that were cleared and failed to prosecute those who had perpetrated the acts of violence.
While the ICJ recognised the role Arsa played, it found there was "overlap" between an "anti-Rohingya hate speech campaign" - which portrayed the Rohingya as "sub-human" and "a violent threat" - and the clearance operations that made violence against the population more likely.
Myanmar consistently denied genocide against the Rohingya, saying its operations had targeted militant or insurgent threats in response to the Arsa attacks.
In January, government representative Ko Ko Hlaing told the ICJ that the country "was not obliged to remain idle and allow terrorists to have free reign". He said he had "no comment" following Thursday's verdict.
The ICJ also looked at the wider treatment of Rohingya leading up to the clearance operation and found that policies like limiting married couples to two children were discriminatory and aimed to erode their rights.
It said Myanmar had an obligation to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure could be determined at a later date.
'Recognition of our suffering'
The court's decision was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of Rakhine in 2017 and now lives in Canada. "The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades."
Human Rights Watch said the ruling was "long-awaited recognition of the suffering the Rohingya have endured".
Meanwhile, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said the "suffering, misery and humiliation" inflicted on the Rohingya people was a "stain on the conscience of humanity". He added that the court's decision "must now translate into real action".
To implicate the Myanmar government in genocide, the court had to determine not just that terrible acts had been committed, but that there was an intent on the part of officials or arms of the state to partially or completely destroy the group.
Thursday's ruling is without precedent. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ICJ has only twice before ruled on claims of state-backed genocide in the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in the aftermath of the Holocaust, in both cases finding there was insufficient evidence to attribute the actions to the state.
Dozens of individuals have been found guilty of genocide, but finding their actions were at the direct behest of the state requires a higher evidential bar to prove genocide, the gravest of crimes under international law.
Philippe Sands KC, a top human rights lawyer who helped bring the case, described it as an "historic judgment".
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One programme that it was "right up there with the great moments of international justice: Nuremberg, Pinochet, and others", referring to the trials of Nazi leaders following World War Two and that of the Chilean dictator, respectively.
However, the ICJ is not a criminal court and its powers of enforcement are limited. It cannot send military officials to prison, while it relies on the UN Security Council and political pressure to impose its rulings.
The ruling will, though, have implications for other genocide cases pending with the ICJ, including one brought by South Africa against Israel over its war in Gaza.
Sands said that pending case had been the "elephant in the room" during the Myanmar hearings.

Trump’s CISA nominee denies Capitol was attacked on Jan. 6
Two senators subsequently said they would place holds on the nominee, who also refused to acknowledge Biden's 2020 electoral victory.
Updated: 3:33 p.m. ET.
President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency denied Thursday that the U.S. Capitol building was attacked on Jan. 6, 2021, and refused to say who won the 2020 presidential election.
Michael LoSapio, who is currently Palantir’s chief information security officer, made the remarks during his confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee, where Democrats also pressed him on whether he would seek to reverse staffing and budget cuts at the government’s main civilian cyberdefense agency.
“No, I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio told Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., after initially saying he did not know. When Blumenthal asked again whether the Capitol had been attacked, LoSapio answered no.
“I wasn’t involved in politics,” he said. “I know what I saw on the news.”
Trump supporters stormed the Capitol that day, assaulting hundreds of police officers and interrupting Congress’ certification of then-President Joe Biden’s victory. Biden won both the popular vote and the Electoral College in 2020.
Earlier in the exchange, Blumenthal asked LoSapio to identify the popular-vote winner.
“I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago,” LoSapio said. Pressed further, he said his only involvement in that election was voting for Trump.
[Update: Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said they plan to place holds on LoSapio's nomination, adding a significant bipartisan obstacle to filling a leadership vacancy that has stretched nearly two years.]
Congressional reports and law enforcement findings widely characterize the events of January 6 as a violent riot aimed at disrupting the certification of the 2020 election results. Explicitly denying that the Capitol was attacked is a major departure from the documented record of the day’s events, particularly for a nominee seeking to lead an agency tasked in part with protecting U.S. elections.
The refusal to acknowledge Biden's electoral victory is also notable. CISA drew Trump’s ire in 2020, when the agency rejected his false claims that the election was stolen, and he fired its first director, Chris Krebs, for publicly declaring the election secure.
In his second term, Trump expanded his election denialism, and LoSapio's responses echoed those of other presidential nominees. On Wednesday, Trump’s pick for a federal appeals court position declined to answer who won the 2020 election and told senators that answering such questions could be an ethical violation.
A Palantir spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment.
If confirmed, LoSapio would inherit an agency that has lost roughly one-third of its workforce since Trump returned to office, gone without a Senate-confirmed director and reduced assistance to state and local offices. Some election officials said the cuts have left them without trusted federal contacts and disrupted preparations for the midterms.
Acting Director Nick Andersen has since worked to rebuild some of the staffing.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., asked LoSapio whether he supported the administration’s cuts, citing the loss of about 1,000 positions and a proposed budget roughly $385 million below the agency’s 2025 funding.
LoSapio said he could not assess CISA’s current condition from outside government and would examine its needs before deciding whether to seek more money.
“I don’t necessarily believe more money means more security,” he said. “I believe spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk.”
When asked whether he would replace departed staff, LoSapio again said he needed to assess the agency first.
“I’m going to investigate and dig in and understand where our gaps are,” he said, adding that he would request more resources if needed.
In his written opening statement, LoSapio outlined four priorities: defending civilian federal agencies, supporting infrastructure operators and state and local governments, reducing weaknesses in technology products, and recruiting and retaining staff.
His nomination follows nearly two years without a permanent Senate-confirmed CISA director. Jen Easterly left in January 2025, and Andersen has led the agency in an acting capacity since February. Trump’s previous nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew in April.
Some industry officials told Nextgov/FCW ahead of the hearing that they were uncertain about LoSapio’s plans and had hoped Andersen would receive the nomination. Others welcomed the prospect of permanent leadership.
The White House has defended LoSapio’s selection, citing his technical experience and work protecting Palantir against nation-state threats.
If confirmed, LoSapio would face Democratic majorities in both chambers next year. Lawmakers have already pledged to investigate CISA’s workforce cuts and changes to its election security work, among other things.

One of the UK's largest oil refinery operators has been ordered to pay Â£873,473 after breaching environmental permit limits nearly 500 times over three years.
The Environment Agency (EA) said the Stanlow refinery in Ellesmere Port, Cheshire, exceeded wastewater discharge limits at least 489 times between 2018 and 2020. Essar Oil (UK) Limited pleaded guilty to 12 charges in March.
Essar Oil, which trades as EET Fuels, was fined Â£800,000 and ordered to pay Â£73,473 in costs at Warrington Magistrates' Court.
EET Fuels said it regretted the "historic incidents" and had invested more than Â£24m to improve environmental performance.
Ten charges related to wastewater discharges containing oil, suspended solids and chemicals, including cyanide, into Thornton Brook, the River Gowy and the Manchester Ship Canal.
Two other charges concerned incidents in 2019.
In February 2019, between 15 and 20 tonnes of a chemical leaked into the ship canal after a vent was left open and a written procedure was not followed.
A month later, a contractor's vehicle ruptured an effluent pipe. During repairs, about 15 tonnes of partially treated sewage entered Thornton Brook, which leads to the protected Mersey Estuary.
Environment Agency officers reported a sheen of oil on local waterways, while vegetation downstream of the refinery's discharge point was blackened by oil in January 2020.
The company was fined Â£80,000 for each of the 10 offences, with no additional penalty for the two 2019 incidents. Three breaches from 2022 and 2023 were taken into consideration without further punishment.
Nigel Glasgow, the Environment Agency's area environment manager, said the case showed "a repeated failure to comply" with permit conditions.
An EET Fuels spokesperson said: "We take our environmental responsibilities extremely seriously and regret these historic incidents."
The company said its investment included rerouting wastewater to United Utilities' Ellesmere Port treatment works, resulting in "a significant improvement in environmental performance", including fewer discharges and reduced freshwater use.

aebbb29b68e6.text: By — Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press By — Jessica Hill, Associated Press Jessica Hill, Associated Press By — Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/iowans-brace-for-lead-dust-cloud-as-army-plans-to-detonate-5-tons-of-bomb-making-chemicals Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Iowans brace for lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals Nation Nov 19, 2026 2:41 PM EST DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Plans by the U.S. Army to detonate about 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals that have become unusable and might explode if moved have residents in southeast Iowa worried that a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems. READ MORE: Notre Dame fire wakes the world up to dangers of lead dust The detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is set for Friday, and officials recommend that some residents in nearby Middletown begin vacating the area that morning. If they can't leave their homes, they should stay inside and keep windows and doors closed. "The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground," an advisory states. "Lead is toxic to humans and animals. The goal of this advisory is to provide the public with actionable information out of an abundance of caution to minimize lead exposure." Officials have released maps showing the potential drift north, and the Army will continue to update the maps based on weather. Some schools in the region have already canceled classes. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, but thousands more could be affected. The vibrations from the two blasts will be quick but could break old windows in town. The resulting dust is expected to linger for no more than one hour, depending on wind speed, officials said. While the Army recommends cleaning cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces, residents have taken to social media to voice concern and question whether that will be enough. Surrounding communities get late notice Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of several dozen barrels containing lead azide, after the ammunition plant paused operations as part of a review and the degraded material was discovered. "The safety of our people and our neighbors is non‑negotiable," Lt. Col. Daniel Nosse, commander of the plant, said at the time, acknowledging the volatility of the chemical compound used in munitions production. The Army shared more details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, advising that a detonation was planned for an unspecified date in November. The Environmental Protection Agency on Nov. 13 approved an emergency permit, paving the way for Friday's detonation. That permit required the Army to model the pathway for specific amounts of lead that could be dispersed in the air and deposited on the ground, notifying the public five days in advance. That prompted Sunday's advisory to communities as far as 100 miles (160 kilometers) away. Just a few miles northwest, Danville Community School District will close Friday, the superintendent said in an announcement Tuesday. Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but there were enough uncertainties that made canceling "the most responsible decision." "I am not suggesting that the detonation will result in unsafe conditions," he wrote. "The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon." In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles (32 kilometers) northeast, city officials were approached about allowing soil, water and air testing late last month. But they only learned of their potential exposure on Sunday, when the initial map put them in the center of the dust exposure area. Schools and the public library will close Friday and the local fire department planned to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles. The city of nearly 2,000 residents was no longer expected to be affected based on an updated map. "This is probably a first for me. I believe it's a first for a lot of our citizens," Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker said Wednesday. "The biggest issue we're having is the lack of information." Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office was first briefed Monday on the public advisory, her office said. News of the planned blasts also caught the attention of environmental and public health officials in Illinois. They urged the U.S. military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state following the detonations. Long-term storage leaves lead azide vulnerable The barrels of lead azide had been stored at the ammunition plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, public affairs specialist at the Army Sustainment Command. During a routine check earlier this year, they found that some of the water had evaporated, causing the lead azide to crystallize. That makes it more sensitive to friction and shock, thus "creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation," according to an emergency permit approved last week by the EPA. Moving or relocating it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, officials said. Barati said that possibility increases in cold weather. "We're really concerned about the weather situation," Barati said on moving forward with Friday's detonation. "We're really concerned that it will detonate on its own." The Army said it put together a panel of experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with the detonation plan. The barrels are surrounded above, below and on all sides with concrete, which is buried under soil. Sand barriers are stacked two stories high around the soil. (AP) — Democratic lawmakers in Mississippi are calling for an investigation after a spike in the number of people listed as inactive on voter rolls before this year's midterm elections — an increase of nearly 60,000 since the presidential election two years ago. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The shift apparently was caused by the integration of data from Experian, one of the major credit reporting agencies, into the voter roll maintenance process. It came before a historic election for Democrats, who unseated one of the Deep South state's Republican senators. The lawmakers want an investigation and legislation to ensure that eligible voters are not mistakenly moved to inactive status, especially as the party tries to maintain its political momentum going into next year's race for governor. "Mississippians did their part. They showed up to vote," said Democratic state Rep. Kabir Karriem, who chairs the Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus. "Now election officials owe them an answer to the most basic question in our democracy: Did my vote count?" During a news conference Thursday, the caucus requested that legislative oversight committees investigate how credit reporting data was used on the voter rolls and called for a public hearing on the matter. Karriem said his caucus wants to know how many voters were marked inactive, what guidance county officials were given on how to use the Experian data and why some provisional ballots cast by those who were marked as inactive were counted while others were not. Caucus leaders also called for changes to the state's voting laws. They are pressing for early voting, for people to have the ability to register to vote online and for a process that allows voters to fix any problems with absentee ballots. They also are seeking to repeal or amend laws that allow the use of third party data in determining a voter's eligibility. WATCH: How Scott Colom won his longshot bid to flip Mississippi's Senate seat The caucus members said the investigation and legislative changes should be completed quickly, before next year's elections for statewide offices, the Legislature and state Supreme Court. "We need urgency, we need accountability and above all we need to restore public trust in our elections," said Democratic state Rep. Zakiya Summers. Democrats are focusing on the issue as they are hoping to build on Democrat Scott Colom's win in the race for U.S. Senate over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. Mississippi added Experian data for verifying addresses Mississippi for years had primarily relied on U.S. Postal Service change of address data to maintain its voter rolls. In 2025, Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson announced a partnership with Experian, one of the country's three major credit reporting agencies, that was intended to "strengthen the integrity" of the state's elections. Under the agreement, county elections officials were given access to credit and Social Security data. They were to use that in addition to Postal Service data to verify voters' addresses. Mississippi law requires election officials to move voters whose addresses are questioned in the vetting process to inactive status at the same time they mail them a confirmation card, which voters can use to reestablish their active status. Other states do it differently: Policies in Delaware, Maryland, Oklahoma and Rhode Island generally allow voters time to respond to the notice before their status is changed to inactive, according to the MIT Election Data and Science Lab. Mississippi's process meant voters may not have known they had been switched to inactive until they showed up to vote, forcing them to cast a provisional ballot. The number of Mississippi voters listed as "inactive" was 185,000 during the 2022 midterm elections and 171,000 during the presidential election two years ago, according to Associated Press data. Before this year's election, more than 230,000 people were marked as inactive, according to the secretary of state, after the Experian data was included in the verification process. Colom won the race for Senate against Hyde-Smith by a fraction of that amount. Just over 8,000 votes separated the candidates with 99% of ballots counted. State moves on from Experian Elizabeth Jonson, a spokesperson for the secretary of state's office, said the 230,000 figure was "accumulated over more than five years of maintenance by local officials" and that the state does not classify voters as inactive solely based on the Experian data. The rise in the number of inactive voters this year was caused by integrating Experian data into the overall verification process, Watson said. In a social media video, Watson said the state had started using data from a new vendor, Interactive Data, which draws on information from all three major credit bureaus, to maintain its voter rolls. WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is important for talking, too.
Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.
The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word. 
A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”
The new research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.
The finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, says neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”
Scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.
Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” said UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.
Some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”
Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.
The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang said.

c912d06b9259.text: By — Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/nasas-voyager-1-calls-earth-from-more-than-16-billion-miles-or-one-light-day-away Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter NASA's Voyager 1 calls Earth from more than 16 billion miles, or one light-day, away Science Nov 19, 2026 1:51 PM EST CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — NASA's Voyager 1 has phoned home from one light-day away, humanity's first emissary to cross this monumental threshold way out in interstellar space. Flight controllers received the spacecraft's call Thursday, exactly 24 hours after it was sent. That's how long it took for the radio signal to traverse the more than 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) at the speed of light. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler," NASA's Joe Westlake, the heliophysics division director, said in a statement. It marked another day in the history books for Voyager 1, which launched in 1977. It swept past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, snapped the most distant photo ever taken of our "Pale Blue Dot" in 1990, became the most distant human-made object in 1998, and crossed from the sun's sphere of influence into the vast void between stars in 2012. NASA could not confirm this newest distance record until the signal reached the control team at California's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. But that didn't stop the space agency from wishing everyone a "Happy Voyager light-day … day!" via social media the day before. "Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," JPL director Dave Gallagher said in a statement. READ MORE: Voyager 1 is now a light-day from Earth. Here's what to know about NASA's longest-running mission Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, are NASA's longest-operating space missions, still churning out data despite powering down most of their instruments to keep exploring. Voyager 2 actually beat its twin into space by two weeks. But its route to Jupiter and Saturn plus Uranus and Neptune was slower and longer, and it did not reach interstellar space until 2018. It won't reach the one-light-day mark until 2035. Both spacecraft are doing well for their 49 years of age, plowing through space at 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) with plutonium for power. Picture-taking ended long ago, but they typically send back bits of precious data almost every day on their never-before-explored environment. No science or engineering data have been received from Voyager 1 since Saturday, according to NASA. However, the carrier signal that normally conveys that data kept coming and, along with flight path calculations, allowed the team to confirm the light-day milestone. Controllers are trying to figure out why the flow of science and engineering data stopped. Each carries a so-called Golden Record brimming with the sounds of Earth. The project was led by the late Cornell University astronomer Carl Sagan, who also coined the phrase "Pale Blue Dot" for Voyager 1's farewell glimpse of Earth. NASA expects the gold-plated phonographic records — time capsules for anyone or anything that might encounter them — to last more than 1 billion years. When refinery operators went on strike to demand safer conditions at a renewable fuels facility northeast of San Francisco in April, they worried that workers brought in to replace them hadn’t been adequately trained to run their potentially explosive processing units. The strikers’ concerns grew as they saw unusually frequent and intense flaring, giant flames shooting up from stacks that burn flammable gases to prevent explosions—a sign of problems inside the plant.
California inspectors confirmed workers’ concerns last month. The state’s Division of Occupational Safety and Health, known as Cal/OSHA, cited Marathon for several violations. Among the most serious was the failure “to train each employee before starting work in a newly assigned process” and “provide the training curriculum … and training certification for newly assigned employees,” documents reviewed by Inside Climate News reveal.
Marathon USW Local 5 members raised their safety concerns during months of contract negotiations with the company, which rejected workers’ proposals to address fatigue from relentless overtime shifts resulting from chronic understaffing. The strike turned into a lockout in June, when Marathon rebuffed the union’s unconditional return-to-work offer.
Operators’ fears about safety emerged as soon as they left the plant to go on strike at midnight on April 27. They realized the people who were taking over their shift had not been trained on their units, said Nick Plurkowski, United Steelworkers Local 5 president. “We had safety concerns with the way the shift turnovers went,” he said.
Plurkowski called Cal/OSHA the next day to outline the workers’ concerns.
Now the workers are even more concerned about inadequate operator training and oversight of the plant’s volatile operations, which they blamed for the catastrophic accident that nearly killed their co-worker Jerome Serrano three years ago on Nov. 19.
The federal agency that investigates the causes of industrial accidents agreed with the workers.
Marathon Martinez’s failure to identify problems with the furnace that processes flammable materials or properly label equipment led to the explosion that enveloped Serrano in a fireball, the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board concluded in March 2025.
“Inadequate operating procedures and operator training for safe burner operation and inadequate engineering controls for operators to identify combustion issues inside the fired heater also contributed to the incident,” the board concluded in its final report.
Workers decided to walk out a year later, saying Marathon rejected their proposals to address safety concerns and refused to offer them the same terms it had negotiated with the national bargaining units that covered more than 30,000 workers across the petroleum and renewables industry.
Cal/OSHA found many of the same problems identified by the Chemical Safety Board over the course of several inspections between April and October. Inspectors determined that at least a dozen employees hadn’t received proper training, including two shift supervisors and 10 operators.
Martinez Renewables has appealed the citations to the state Occupational Safety and Health Appeals Board, said Marathon Petroleum Corp. spokesperson Jamal Kheiry. “We continue to staff the Martinez Renewables facility with highly qualified Marathon personnel, including supervisors, engineers and technical experts with extensive experience and training in safe, reliable plant operations,” Kheiry said. The company looks forward to working with state officials “to resolve the alleged violations,” he said.
Denisse Gómez, a Cal/OSHA spokesperson, confirmed that Marathon appealed the citations. She said the agency is unable to comment on the findings while the appeal is pending.
Altogether, Cal/OSHA cited Marathon for 10 violations, including three classified as serious: inadequate training, uninsulated high-temperature equipment and faulty emergency eyewash stations.

Other violations include failures to provide warning labels on fuel-storage containers; inaccessible fire extinguishers; potential tripping and electrocution hazards; and lack of a heat-illness prevention plan that provides adequate shade, breaks and water for employees loading railcars outside or performing strenuous tasks in rubber suits in high-heat areas. Inspectors spoke with employees who did not know how to acclimate to hot working conditions, as required by California’s heat-illness prevention standard.
Those precautions are critical in refineries, which rely on high heat for processing fuels. California requires pipes or other surfaces that reach 140 degrees Fahrenheit to be insulated to limit harm from accidental contact. Inspectors found uninsulated equipment with average heat readings exceeding 550 degrees F.
That finding outraged Plurkowski, who wondered how workers are supposed to stay safe while doing hour-long tasks while sweating nonstop and standing a foot away from a surface that will melt their skin if they touch it.
While those types of safety issues must be corrected, he said, it’s the lack of training that’s most troubling.
Cal/OSHA “yellow tagged” the unit that burned Serrano, which prohibited anyone from running it until the agency could confirm that employees were sufficiently qualified to operate it safely. Violating a yellow tag results in fines, jail or both.
But the units were tagged only because of “Jerome’s horrific accident,” Plurkowski said. “I just asked OSHA today if they would yellow tag a unit due to lack of training, and they said probably not.”
He asked because he believes the amount of flaring coming from the plant means things are not running smoothly.

4e1f7d6a2cb4.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press By — Barry Hatton, Associated Press Barry Hatton, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/kushner-says-russia-is-comfortable-with-nato-like-security-guarantees-for-ukraine-to-end-war-after-trump-talks-with-putin Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Kushner says Russia is 'comfortable' with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end war after Trump talks with Putin World Nov 19, 2026 1:32 PM EST BERLIN (AP) — U.S. envoy Jared Kushner on Thursday said Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war as it nears the five-year mark. Another American envoy, Steve Witkoff, said U.S. President Donald Trump discussed Ukraine and a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral talks with the Russian and Chinese leaders earlier Thursday. READ MORE: For Putin, sharing a spotlight with Trump and Xi boosts his profile on the global stage Kushner and Witkoff met with European allies in Berlin to discuss their support for Ukraine after a third Ukrainian aerial attack in four days on the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Russian-held Crimea halted rail traffic across the span, officials said Thursday, after earlier strikes shut down the road section of the landmark that is a symbol of Moscow's invasion. Train traffic across the bridge stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti. The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and Trump, as well as to demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable. The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between Kushner, Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort and fear being sidelined by Trump's direct talks with Putin. The American leader called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said. Putin acknowledges the damage and vows to strike back "We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that," Putin told reporters in Shenzhen, China. He insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered the bridge closed to the transport of military hardware or ammunition. Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been "seriously damaged" but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section is believed to be stronger than the road side, to bear the greater weight of cargo wagons. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops. It is a potent reminder of Russia's illegal annexation of the territory and has been a prime target for Ukraine. A large section of the road deck and an arch collapsed in the culmination of weeks of preparatory strikes over seven stages of the operation, according to Zelenskyy, and the train track was damaged by domestically produced Neptune missiles, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said. Now Russia will need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where "our drones are waiting for the cargo," the ministry said. A Ukrainian attack on Russia's Saratov region killed three people and wounded two others, local Gov. Roman Busargin said, and a drone killed a woman traveling by bicycle with her 8-year-old grandson in the Bryansk region, Gov. Egor Kovalchuk said. Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations. Explosions and sirens rang out across Kyiv during the day, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies sustained minor damage, officials said. Two people, including a 44-year-old woman, were killed and at least 23 people, including a 12-year-old boy, were reported wounded as Russian strikes caused damage in 12 regions. But Kyiv's defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances. Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine's resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv's domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries. Kyiv fears Trump and Putin may try to decide Ukraine's fate In China, Trump called Putin "my friend." The American president's relationship with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has soured. European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy. Ukrainian officials fear their country's fate could be determined by agreements between Trump and Putin, while European governments are alarmed by Moscow's aggression. The question of U.S. support for Ukraine, severely curtailed under Trump, could be raised by Democrats in Congress after their wins in the midterm elections. 9eac88092d30.text: President Trump said in a brief phone interview Thursday that he won't make a determination on his next step in the Iran war until the new year. "I am not rushing into any decision [on Iran]. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year," Trump told Axios from Air Force One, on his way back to the U.S. from China. Why it matters: The president's comments come as he faces heavy pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to unleash a decisive bombing campaign soon. Yes, but: Trump could change his mind at any moment. And he wouldn't telegraph plans for an imminent attack even if that's what he was intending to do. A day before the war began in February, Trump said he hadn't made a decision, when in fact he had already ordered strikes. Between the lines: Trump's stated timing could mean he's giving more time for the naval blockade and the economic pressure campaign to play out, as many of his advisers and leaders of Gulf countries are urging. But it could also indicate that if Iran doesn't make concessions by the end of the year, Trump wants to leave himself enough time for military action before the new Democratic-controlled Congress settles in. Driving the news: While stating last week that a major new round of strikes on Iran was " quite unlikely ," Trump is still considering a joint attack with Israel, Axios reported on Wednesday. The president's deliberations are likely to pick up when he returns from Asia. Any U.S. operation would involve Israel and could include strikes on suspected Iranian nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain. Bridges and power plants could also be targeted, as well as Iranian military and civilian leaders. Behind the scenes: The White House has asked the Pentagon and intelligence experts for their assessments of how Iran would respond to each of the strike scenarios the U.S. military has prepared, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. The White House has asked whether any of the options would avoid triggering a devastating Iranian retaliation against Gulf countries' oil and gas facilities. The intrigue: The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad, Roman Gofman, visited Washington and Miami last week for talks with CIA Director John Ratcliffe and White House envoy Steve Witkoff. Gofman, one of Netanyahu's closest confidants, was sent by the Israeli prime minister to press for resuming the war against Iran, an Israeli source said. The Mossad director relayed Israel's concerns about Iranian activities related to chemical weapons development, U.S. and Israeli sources said. Israel claims it has intelligence showing that Iran has stepped up its research and development of chemical weapons as well as conducted tests. Trump was briefed about this new intelligence, a U.S. official said.

7feba83eae79.text: By — Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press By — Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Kelvin Chan, Associated Press By — Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/are-tech-disruptions-and-and-outages-the-new-normal Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Are tech disruptions and and outages the new normal? Nation Nov 19, 2026 1:21 PM EST Inaccessible email inboxes. Banking delays. And a communications meltdown that grounded airplanes for hours, followed by waves of other travel disruptions. In an increasingly interconnected world, some fear such disruptions could be the new normal. READ MORE: Duffy keeps blaming L3Harris after FAA ground stop, even as cause remains unknown Over the past week alone, problems that appeared to emerge from routine updates, security patches or other malfunctions surfaced at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Apple, and even the U.S. government's Federal Aviation Administration and National Security Agency. The Trump administration said there was "zero" indication the latest outages are linked, or caused by bad actors like cybercriminals. The era of artificial intelligence has also raised the stakes for internet security overall. As AI tools uncover new vulnerabilities, many other companies and institutions are racing to patch them before they can be targeted by hackers, a cat-and-mouse game that can lead to a different set of glitches. Social media platforms have been abuzz with a mixture of annoyance, confusion, conspiracy theories and jokes about the string of outages. "To see several disruptions this close together, I think to a lot of people it's made them realize how many parts of their lives they've handed over to these systems that we still, at this point, don't fully understand," Jake Smith, a content creator who regularly posts videos about politics on platforms like Instagram and YouTube, said in an interview. "I think it gives people a sense of helplessness to see all of it happening concurrently in a way." What's gone offline recently Outages and technology errors have piled up across sectors. Late last week, a global Microsoft outage disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business and everyday services into disarray worldwide. Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. Microsoft cited, in part, a failure during a recent upgrade to its servers, spanning from what the company later determined was a "latent defect" in a network fix it had begun deploying over the summer. For air travel, a separate malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years on Friday. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers cancelled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days later, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights on Monday. Online banking troubles also piled up on Monday. JPMorgan Chase said a software bug affected its internal hardware systems — causing transactional delays for its customers and others sending money to related accounts, sending jitters throughout the financial system before the problem was resolved. WATCH: What a string of tech problems reveals about America's digital vulnerabilities And on Tuesday, Apple, Marriott and the NSA joined the growing list. Apple Music, the App Store and AppleCare services were temporarily disrupted after the company said an internal update caused outages. And Marriott said a technical issue also caused problems for sign-ins on its website and app. Meanwhile, the NSA said an internal network it uses to communicate classified information was also offline Tuesday "during scheduled routine maintenance." The government — as well as Microsoft, United, JPMorgan Chase, Apple and Marriott — have again maintained there's no evidence of these disruptions being linked or related to a cyberattack. Microsoft also noted that its outage did not span from "AI / agents." It didn't specify the goal of the network fix it first deployed over the summer. A press contact for Microsoft didn't immediately have further information to share when reached by The Associated Press. The other companies also did not provide additional comments Wednesday about their disruptions when contacted by the AP via email. AI has helped identify vulnerabilities, but also adds to risks AI has nonetheless come into the spotlight as experts evaluate these disruptions — both between heightened risks posed by the technology as well as its ability to detect security gaps. For example, AI recently helped detect sweeping vulnerabilities for PHP, a general-purpose scripting language that powers websites around the world — leading to urgent calls for updates. And that security work has resulted in some limited outages and service delays. President Donald Trump's director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, pointed directly to patching those security gaps when discussing the NSA's outage this week. Clayton told Fox News that the patching following last month's PHP alert has caused some systems to "not come back up" as expected. "That is what has happened at the NSA today," he said. Meanwhile, also this week, cybersecurity startup Calif said it used AI to help uncover a software bug in Java, one of the world's most widely used programming languages and crucial for many big companies. Oracle, which owns Java, later released a security update and U.S. cyber authorities issued an advisory on Wednesday urging organizations to install it. At the same time, others warn that the AI boom could open the door to additional disruptions. READ MORE: Could everything be broken?
